Generative Models

Lesson text (draft) · Teacher's sheet

The filter that was sure of everything

For twenty-three lessons, every filter you built did the same kind of thing. It looked at labelled messages and drew a boundary: a threshold, a halfspace, a tree of questions, a margin, a nearest neighbour. Junk on one side, keep on the other. The learner never asked where the messages came from. It only asked where to put the line.

This week a colleague, Ines, walks over with a different idea. “Stop drawing boundaries,” she says. “Junk is written by people who want something from you. Keep mail is written by colleagues who want lunch. Each kind of message is produced in its own way, word by word. So let’s learn how each kind is produced. When a new message arrives, we ask: which of the two producers most likely wrote this?”

It is a lovely idea, and she has already built it. For each word in the dictionary, she counts how often it appears in junk and how often in keep. Those fractions become her estimates of how each producer behaves. A new message gets a score under each producer, and the filter picks the larger one.

On Monday the filter is brilliant on ordinary mail. On Tuesday the bug reports arrive, and they are strange. A message that reads like a textbook prize draw, “free”, “click”, “claim your prize”, was filed as keep with probability exactly 1. Not 0.99. One. Another message, containing the word “winner”, did not get filed at all: the filter threw an exception and the message sat in limbo. When you look closer, the pattern is always the same. Every message that misbehaves contains some word the filter had never seen in one of the two piles. One unseen word, and the filter goes from “probably” to absolute certainty, or to a crash.

How can counting words, the most honest estimate imaginable, produce a filter that is certain of nonsense? And what would it mean to count correctly? This lesson builds the answer from the ground up. Along the way you will meet the most popular estimation principle in all of statistics, and find out that it is a learning rule you already know in disguise.

Telling the story of a message

Let’s name the two approaches before we look at Ines’s numbers.

Every filter in lessons 2 to 23 followed the discriminative approach: the goal is a hypothesis that labels messages accurately, and nothing more. We never tried to say how likely a given message is to arrive; we only asked which side of a boundary it lands on. Lesson 3 made one big promise about this approach: it is distribution free, meaning the guarantees hold for every distribution D\mathcal DD over messages and labels, with no assumption at all about its shape.

The generative approach makes the opposite bet. It assumes the distribution D\mathcal DD has a specific form described by a handful of numbers, called parameters, and its goal is to estimate those parameters from the training sequence. A distribution described this way is a parametric model, and estimating its parameters from data is called parametric density estimation. Ines’s model has one parameter per word and per kind of message: the probability that a message of that kind contains that word.

Why would anyone take the generative route, when it means assuming more? A principle usually credited to the statistician Vladimir Vapnik warns against it: when solving a given problem, try to avoid a more general problem as an intermediate step. Learning the whole distribution is a more general problem than learning to label, and usually a harder one. But there are good reasons to try anyway. If you do learn the distribution, you can predict with the Bayes optimal predictor of lesson 3. (A reminder: that is the hypothesis that gives every message whichever label is more probable for it, and no hypothesis has smaller true risk.) Sometimes estimating the parameters is computationally easier than finding a good discriminative hypothesis. And sometimes there is no single task yet: you want a model of the mail you can query later for questions nobody has asked, or one a person can read and understand.

[diagram:generative: built on the lesson page]

So the question of this lesson is: how should you estimate the parameters, and what can you promise about the result?

Ines’s filter, by hand

Let’s rebuild Ines’s filter on a dictionary small enough to hold in your head. It has seven words: “free”, “prize”, “click”, “invoice”, “meeting”, “lunch” and “winner”. A message is described by which of these words it contains, one yes/no feature per word, just as messages were vectors of yes/no features in lesson 1. Label 1 is junk and 0 is keep.

Your users labelled eight messages, four of each kind:

messagewordslabel
1free, prize, clickjunk
2free, clickjunk
3prize, clickjunk
4free, prizejunk
5meeting, lunchkeep
6invoice, meetingkeep
7lunch, clickkeep
8free, lunch, meetingkeep

Ines estimates, for each word and each label, the fraction of messages with that label that contain the word. Call the estimate for word jjj and label yyy by the name θ^j,y\hat\theta_{j,y}θ^j,y​. The hat on top is the usual mark for “estimated from data”, and θ\thetaθ (the Greek letter theta) is the usual letter for a parameter. Count before you read on: what is θ^invoice,1\hat\theta_{\text{invoice},1}θ^invoice,1​, the fraction of the junk messages that contain “invoice”?

None of the four junk messages contains it, so the fraction is 0/4=00/4 = 00/4=0. Here is the full table.

wordin junk θ^j,1\hat\theta_{j,1}θ^j,1​in keep θ^j,0\hat\theta_{j,0}θ^j,0​

Now her scoring recipe. A producer of junk writes a message by flipping one biased coin per word: word jjj goes in with probability θj,1\theta_{j,1}θj,1​, and stays out with probability 1−θj,11 - \theta_{j,1}1−θj,1​, each coin independent of the others. So the probability that the junk producer writes exactly the message xxx is a product of seven factors, one per word. Writing xj=1x_j = 1xj​=1 when word jjj is in the message and xj=0x_j = 0xj​=0 when it is not:

P[x∣y]=∏j=1dθj,y xj (1−θj,y)1−xj.\mathbb P[x \mid y] = \prod_{j=1}^{d} \theta_{j,y}^{\,x_j} \, (1 - \theta_{j,y})^{1 - x_j}.P[x∣y]=j=1∏d​θj,yxj​​(1−θj,y​)1−xj​.

This is the first formula of the lesson, so let’s take it apart from the inside out.

  • ddd is the number of words in the dictionary, here 7, and jjj runs over them: j=1j = 1j=1 is “free”, j=2j = 2j=2 is “prize”, and so on.
  • θj,y\theta_{j,y}θj,y​ is the probability that a message with label yyy contains word jjj. The two subscripts say which word and which label.
  • θj,y xj(1−θj,y)1−xj\theta_{j,y}^{\,x_j} (1 - \theta_{j,y})^{1 - x_j}θj,yxj​​(1−θj,y​)1−xj​ is a compact way to write a choice. If xj=1x_j = 1xj​=1, the exponents are 1 and 0, and since anything to the power 0 is 1, the factor is θj,y\theta_{j,y}θj,y​: the chance the word went in. If xj=0x_j = 0xj​=0, it is 1−θj,y1 - \theta_{j,y}1−θj,y​: the chance it stayed out.
  • ∏j=1d\prod_{j=1}^{d}∏j=1d​ (a capital Greek pi) means “multiply together, for jjj from 1 to ddd”. It is to multiplication what ∑\sum∑ is to addition. We may multiply because the coins are independent: the probability that several independent things all happen is the product of their probabilities.
  • P[x∣y]\mathbb P[x \mid y]P[x∣y] is read “the probability of xxx given yyy”: the vertical bar means “given”, so this is the chance of writing exactly message xxx if the writer is the producer of kind yyy.

In one sentence: the chance that the producer of kind yyy writes exactly this message is the product, over every dictionary word, of the chance that it put that word in or left it out, as the message says.

Push message 2, “free, click”, through the junk producer. “free” is in: 3/43/43/4. “prize” is out: 1−3/4=1/41 - 3/4 = 1/41−3/4=1/4. “click” is in: 3/43/43/4. The four words with θ^=0\hat\theta = 0θ^=0 are out, each with probability 1−0=11 - 0 = 11−0=1. The product is 34⋅14⋅34=9/64≈0.1406\tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac34 = 9/64 \approx 0.140643​⋅41​⋅43​=9/64≈0.1406.

To decide, Ines also needs the share of junk in the mail, P[y=1]\mathbb P[y = 1]P[y=1]. Users labelled four of each, so she takes 1/21/21/2. Then she compares the two producers with Bayes’ rule, the identity that turns “how likely is this message under each kind” into “how likely is each kind given this message”:

P[y=1∣x]=P[y=1] P[x∣y=1]P[y=1] P[x∣y=1]+P[y=0] P[x∣y=0].\mathbb P[y = 1 \mid x] = \frac{\mathbb P[y = 1]\, \mathbb P[x \mid y = 1]}{\mathbb P[y = 1]\, \mathbb P[x \mid y = 1] + \mathbb P[y = 0]\, \mathbb P[x \mid y = 0]}.P[y=1∣x]=P[y=1]P[x∣y=1]+P[y=0]P[x∣y=0]P[y=1]P[x∣y=1]​.
  • P[y=1]\mathbb P[y = 1]P[y=1] is the share of junk in all mail before you read a word, and P[y=0]=1−P[y=1]\mathbb P[y = 0] = 1 - \mathbb P[y = 1]P[y=0]=1−P[y=1] the share of keep.
  • P[y=1] P[x∣y=1]\mathbb P[y = 1]\,\mathbb P[x \mid y = 1]P[y=1]P[x∣y=1] is the probability that a random message is junk and reads exactly like xxx: first pick the producer, then the producer writes xxx. The second product in the denominator is the same for keep.
  • The denominator adds the two ways xxx could have been produced, so it is the total probability of seeing xxx at all.
  • P[y=1∣x]\mathbb P[y = 1 \mid x]P[y=1∣x], on the left, is the probability that the message is junk, given that it reads exactly like xxx.

In one sentence: the chance that this message is junk is the junk producer’s share of all the ways this message could have come about. For “free, click”, the junk side is 12⋅0.1406=0.0703\tfrac12 \cdot 0.1406 = 0.070321​⋅0.1406=0.0703, the keep side works out to 0.00150.00150.0015, and the filter says junk with probability 0.0703/(0.0703+0.0015)≈0.980.0703/(0.0703 + 0.0015) \approx 0.980.0703/(0.0703+0.0015)≈0.98. That is a sensible answer.

Now try it on two of the messages from the bug reports: “free, click, meeting”, and “winner, click”. Before you run it, predict: what will each side be?

import math
W = ["free", "prize", "click", "invoice",
     "meeting", "lunch", "winner"]
junk = [{"free", "prize", "click"}, {"free", "click"},
        {"prize", "click"}, {"free", "prize"}]
keep = [{"meeting", "lunch"}, {"invoice", "meeting"},
        {"lunch", "click"}, {"free", "lunch", "meeting"}]
def freq(msgs):
    return {w: sum(w in x for x in msgs) / len(msgs) for w in W}
def P(x, th):
    return math.prod(th[w] if w in x else 1 - th[w] for w in W)
th1, th0 = freq(junk), freq(keep)
for x in ({"free", "click"}, {"free", "click", "meeting"},
          {"winner", "click"}):
    p1, p0 = 0.5 * P(x, th1), 0.5 * P(x, th0)
    try:
        post = p1 / (p1 + p0)
        print(round(p1, 4), round(p0, 4), round(post, 2))
    except ZeroDivisionError as err:
        print(round(p1, 4), round(p0, 4), "crash:", err)

It prints:

0.0703 0.0015 0.98
0.0 0.0044 0.0
0.0 0.0 crash: division by zero

There is the bug, reproduced by hand. “free, click, meeting” has two strong junk words, but “meeting” never appeared in the four junk messages, so θ^meeting,1=0\hat\theta_{\text{meeting},1} = 0θ^meeting,1​=0, the junk producer’s product contains a factor 0, and the filter concludes the message is junk with probability exactly 0. And “winner” never appeared anywhere, so both producers give the message probability 0, and Bayes’ rule divides zero by zero.

Notice what went wrong, because it is subtle. The arithmetic is fine. The fractions are honest counts. What failed is the step from counts to probabilities: four junk messages without “meeting” are weak evidence that junk is unlikely to say “meeting”, and Ines’s estimate turned them into a proof that junk can never say it. A single factor of 0 then overrides any amount of evidence from every other word.

Explore it in a bigger mail room. The lab below has a dictionary of 200 words, each with its own true frequency in junk and in keep, many of them rare. You choose how many labelled messages of each kind the filter sees, and watch how often a fresh message makes Ines’s filter certain or makes it crash.

[lab: built on the lesson page]

With 100 labelled messages of each kind, more than a quarter of fresh messages crash the filter and almost half more get an answer of exactly 0 or exactly 1. Rare words are everywhere in real mail, and every one of them is a trap. To fix this properly, we need to understand what Ines was actually computing. It has a name.

Which parameter makes the data most likely?

Forget the filter for a moment and look at one word in one pile: “prize” in the four junk messages. Message 1 contains it, message 2 does not, messages 3 and 4 do. Write that as the pattern 1, 0, 1, 1.

Now play a game. Suppose the true probability that a junk message contains “prize” were some number θ\thetaθ. How likely would it be to see exactly this pattern? Each message is an independent coin, so the chance is θ\thetaθ for message 1, times 1−θ1 - \theta1−θ for message 2, times θ\thetaθ twice more. Try a few values:

θ\thetaθchance of the pattern 1, 0, 1, 1
0.250.0117
0.500.0625
0.750.1055
0.900.0729

Some values of θ\thetaθ make what you actually saw much more plausible than others. A world where “prize” turns up in a quarter of junk would rarely produce three hits out of four; a world where it turns up in three quarters produces them most often of the four we tried. The idea of this section is to choose the parameter that makes the observed data most likely. That is exactly what Ines did, without saying so: 3/43/43/4 is the winner. Let’s make it precise.

The model. We observe one yes/no value per example, x∈{0,1}x \in \{0, 1\}x∈{0,1}, and the model says x=1x = 1x=1 with probability θ\thetaθ, for an unknown θ\thetaθ between 0 and 1. Its probability of each value is

Pθ[x]=θx(1−θ)1−x.P_\theta[x] = \theta^{x} (1 - \theta)^{1 - x}.Pθ​[x]=θx(1−θ)1−x.
  • xxx is one observation: 1 if the word is in the message, 0 if not. The right side is Ines’s exponent trick for a single word.
  • θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0, 1]θ∈[0,1] is the parameter: ∈\in∈ reads “is a member of”, and [0,1][0, 1][0,1] is the set of numbers from 0 to 1, ends included.
  • The subscript in PθP_\thetaPθ​ says which parameter the probability is computed under: the same xxx gets different probabilities under different θ\thetaθ.

In one sentence: under parameter θ\thetaθ, a 1 has probability θ\thetaθ and a 0 has probability 1−θ1 - \theta1−θ. This distribution is called the Bernoulli distribution with parameter θ\thetaθ. With θ=0.75\theta = 0.75θ=0.75, Pθ[1]=0.75P_\theta[1] = 0.75Pθ​[1]=0.75 and Pθ[0]=0.25P_\theta[0] = 0.25Pθ​[0]=0.25.

The likelihood. The training sequence is now just the observations, S=(x1,…,xm)S = (x_1, \dots, x_m)S=(x1​,…,xm​), drawn independently. A reminder from lesson 1: mmm is the number of examples, and the examples are i.i.d., each drawn from the same distribution with no draw influencing another. Multiply the per-example probabilities, and collect the factors. If k=∑i=1mxik = \sum_{i=1}^m x_ik=∑i=1m​xi​ is the number of 1s, there are kkk factors θ\thetaθ and m−km - km−k factors 1−θ1 - \theta1−θ:

Pθ[S]=∏i=1mθxi(1−θ)1−xi=θk(1−θ)m−k.P_\theta[S] = \prod_{i=1}^{m} \theta^{x_i} (1 - \theta)^{1 - x_i} = \theta^{k} (1 - \theta)^{m - k}.Pθ​[S]=i=1∏m​θxi​(1−θ)1−xi​=θk(1−θ)m−k.
  • ∏i=1m\prod_{i=1}^m∏i=1m​ multiplies one factor per example, iii from 1 to mmm. Independence of the examples is what allows the product.
  • k=∑ixik = \sum_i x_ik=∑i​xi​ adds up the observations, so it counts the 1s; m−km - km−k counts the 0s.
  • The right side just groups equal factors: the order of a product does not matter.

In one sentence: the chance of the whole training sequence under θ\thetaθ is θ\thetaθ once per 1 times 1−θ1 - \theta1−θ once per 0. Seen as a function of θ\thetaθ with the data held fixed, Pθ[S]P_\theta[S]Pθ​[S] is called the likelihood of θ\thetaθ. For the “prize” pattern, m=4m = 4m=4, k=3k = 3k=3, and at θ=0.75\theta = 0.75θ=0.75 the likelihood is 0.753⋅0.25=0.10550.75^3 \cdot 0.25 = 0.10550.753⋅0.25=0.1055, the third row of the table.

Products of many probabilities are tiny numbers, and computers dislike tiny numbers: a product of a thousand factors of about 0.5 is smaller than the smallest positive floating-point number, so it rounds to 0. The fix is to take logarithms, which turn products into sums. Throughout this lesson log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm, base eee. Because log⁡\loglog is increasing (a bigger input always gives a bigger output), whichever θ\thetaθ maximizes the likelihood also maximizes its logarithm. The log-likelihood of SSS given θ\thetaθ is

L(S;θ)=log⁡Pθ[S]=klog⁡θ+(m−k)log⁡(1−θ).L(S; \theta) = \log P_\theta[S] = k \log \theta + (m - k) \log(1 - \theta).L(S;θ)=logPθ​[S]=klogθ+(m−k)log(1−θ).
  • L(S;θ)L(S; \theta)L(S;θ) is a number that depends on the data SSS and on the parameter θ\thetaθ; the semicolon separates the data from the parameter. (This LLL has no subscript, unlike the risks LSL_SLS​ and LDL_{\mathcal D}LD​; the context keeps them apart.)
  • log⁡\loglog of a product is the sum of the logs, and log⁡an=nlog⁡a\log a^n = n \log alogan=nloga, so θk\theta^kθk becomes klog⁡θk \log \thetaklogθ and (1−θ)m−k(1-\theta)^{m-k}(1−θ)m−k becomes (m−k)log⁡(1−θ)(m-k)\log(1-\theta)(m−k)log(1−θ).
  • Both logs are of numbers at most 1, so both terms are at most 0: a log-likelihood is never positive for yes/no data.

In one sentence: the log-likelihood adds log⁡θ\log \thetalogθ for each 1 and log⁡(1−θ)\log(1 - \theta)log(1−θ) for each 0. For “prize”, L(S;0.75)=3log⁡0.75+log⁡0.25=−0.863−1.386=−2.249L(S; 0.75) = 3 \log 0.75 + \log 0.25 = -0.863 - 1.386 = -2.249L(S;0.75)=3log0.75+log0.25=−0.863−1.386=−2.249.

Definition (maximum likelihood estimator). The maximum likelihood estimator is a parameter that maximizes the log-likelihood,

θ^∈argmax⁡θL(S;θ).\hat\theta \in \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} L(S; \theta).θ^∈θargmax​L(S;θ).
  • argmax⁡θ\operatorname*{argmax}_\thetaargmaxθ​ of a function is the set of inputs θ\thetaθ at which the function reaches its largest value (“arg” for argument: not the largest value itself, but where it happens).
  • The ∈\in∈ says θ^\hat\thetaθ^ is one of them: if several parameters tie, any of them counts.

In one sentence: the estimate is whichever parameter makes the training sequence most likely. We abbreviate it MLE.

import math
S = [1, 0, 1, 1]
def P(S, th):
    return math.prod(th**x * (1 - th)**(1 - x) for x in S)
def L(S, th):
    k, m = sum(S), len(S)
    return k * math.log(th) + (m - k) * math.log(1 - th)
for th in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9):
    print(th, round(P(S, th), 4), round(L(S, th), 3))
grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(1, 1000)]
print(max(grid, key=lambda th: L(S, th)))

It prints the table above with the log-likelihoods beside it (−4.447-4.447−4.447, −2.773-2.773−2.773, −2.249-2.249−2.249, −2.619-2.619−2.619), and then 0.75: a search over a thousand values of θ\thetaθ lands on Ines’s fraction. That is no accident.

At θ=0.5\theta = 0.5θ=0.5 with k=3k = 3k=3, m=4m = 4m=4, it is 6−2=46 - 2 = 46−2=4: still climbing.

The edge cases. If k=0k = 0k=0, the log-likelihood is mlog⁡(1−θ)m \log(1 - \theta)mlog(1−θ), which is largest at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0, where it equals 0 (the term klog⁡θk \log \thetaklogθ is absent because k=0k = 0k=0; by the usual convention 0⋅log⁡0=00 \cdot \log 0 = 00⋅log0=0). So θ^=0=k/m\hat\theta = 0 = k/mθ^=0=k/m. If k=mk = mk=m, symmetrically θ^=1=k/m\hat\theta = 1 = k/mθ^=1=k/m. ■\blacksquare■

Read that edge case again, because it is our bug. When a word never appears among mmm junk messages, the most likely world, given only those messages, is one where junk never contains it. Maximum likelihood is not making an arithmetic slip: it is answering the question it was asked.

How accurate is it? The estimate θ^\hat\thetaθ^ is an average of mmm independent coins, each equal to 1 with probability θ\thetaθ. An estimator is unbiased when its expected value, averaged over the random training sequence, equals the parameter. This one is, because the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values: ES[θ^]=1m∑iE[xi]=1m⋅mθ=θ\mathbb E_S[\hat\theta] = \frac1m \sum_i \mathbb E[x_i] = \frac1m \cdot m\theta = \thetaES​[θ^]=m1​∑i​E[xi​]=m1​⋅mθ=θ. (A reminder: E\mathbb EE is the expected value, the probability-weighted average, and the subscript SSS says the randomness is in the training sequence.)

Unbiased says the estimate is right on average; it does not say how far one estimate strays. For that, recall Hoeffding’s inequality from lesson 4: for an average Zˉ\bar ZZˉ of mmm i.i.d. variables with values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] and mean μ\muμ, P[∣Zˉ−μ∣>ε]≤2e−2mε2\mathbb P[|\bar Z - \mu| > \varepsilon] \le 2e^{-2m\varepsilon^2}P[∣Zˉ−μ∣>ε]≤2e−2mε2. Set the right side equal to a confidence parameter δ\deltaδ and solve for ε\varepsilonε: 2e−2mε2=δ2e^{-2m\varepsilon^2} = \delta2e−2mε2=δ gives ε=log⁡(2/δ)/(2m)\varepsilon = \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}ε=log(2/δ)/(2m)​. So with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the choice of SSS,

∣θ^−θ∣≤log⁡(2/δ)2m.|\hat\theta - \theta| \le \sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}}.∣θ^−θ∣≤2mlog(2/δ)​​.
  • ∣θ^−θ∣|\hat\theta - \theta|∣θ^−θ∣ is the distance between the estimate and the truth (the bars mean absolute value), and δ\deltaδ is the probability we allow for an unlucky training sequence.
  • Inside the root, log⁡(2/δ)\log(2/\delta)log(2/δ) grows only slowly as you demand more confidence, and the 2m2m2m shrinks the bound as you add examples.

In one sentence: with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, the counted fraction is within log⁡(2/δ)/(2m)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}log(2/δ)/(2m)​ of the true one. With m=500m = 500m=500 messages and δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, that is log⁡40/1000≈0.061\sqrt{\log 40/1000} \approx 0.061log40/1000​≈0.061.

import math, random
m, delta, theta = 500, 0.05, 0.3
eps = math.sqrt(math.log(2 / delta) / (2 * m))
rng, runs, misses = random.Random(0), 2000, 0
for _ in range(runs):
    k = sum(rng.random() < theta for _ in range(m))
    misses += abs(k / m - theta) > eps
print(round(eps, 3), misses / runs)

It prints 0.061 0.0035: the bound promised at most 5% misses, and the simulation saw 0.35%. Hoeffding is honest, and a little pessimistic.

So for estimating the frequency of a word, maximum likelihood is fine: close to the truth with high probability. Keep that in mind. The trouble in Ines’s filter is not that θ^\hat\thetaθ^ is far from θ\thetaθ. It is what happens when a tiny error near 0 gets fed into a logarithm, and we are about to see exactly how.

Measured values: densities

Not every feature is a yes/no word. The mail room also records numbers: the length of a message, the time it was sent. Take the length score of a message, the natural logarithm of its number of characters. It is a real number, and for a real number something odd happens: the probability that a score equals 3.1 exactly, to infinitely many decimals, is 0. So “the probability of the data” is 0 for every parameter, and the likelihood we just defined is useless.

The fix is to use the density instead. A density ppp is a nonnegative function whose area over any interval is the probability of landing in that interval; near a point xxx, the probability of landing in a tiny interval of width www is about p(x)⋅wp(x) \cdot wp(x)⋅w. So a density compares how likely different points are, just as probabilities do for yes/no data. For an i.i.d. sample S=(x1,…,xm)S = (x_1, \dots, x_m)S=(x1​,…,xm​) from a density PθP_\thetaPθ​, define the log-likelihood as the sum of the logs of the density values:

L(S;θ)=log⁡∏i=1mPθ(xi)=∑i=1mlog⁡Pθ(xi).L(S; \theta) = \log \prod_{i=1}^{m} P_\theta(x_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P_\theta(x_i).L(S;θ)=logi=1∏m​Pθ​(xi​)=i=1∑m​logPθ​(xi​).
  • Pθ(xi)P_\theta(x_i)Pθ​(xi​) is the model’s density at the observed value xix_ixi​; the product is the density of the whole independent sample, and the log turns it into a sum.

In one sentence: the log-likelihood of measured data adds up the log of the model’s density at each observed value. The maximum likelihood estimator is again a maximizer of L(S;θ)L(S; \theta)L(S;θ). To keep notation light, from here on we write P[X=x]\mathbb P[X = x]P[X=x], or Pθ[x]P_\theta[x]Pθ​[x], for both the probability of xxx (yes/no data) and the density at xxx (measured data).

The Gaussian model. Lengths of keep messages cluster around a typical value, with fewer messages the further you go. The usual model for such a bell-shaped spread is the Gaussian (or normal) distribution with parameters θ=(μ,σ)\theta = (\mu, \sigma)θ=(μ,σ), whose density is

Pθ(x)=1σ2πexp⁡(−(x−μ)22σ2).P_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).Pθ​(x)=σ2π​1​exp(−2σ2(x−μ)2​).
  • μ\muμ (mu) is the centre of the bell, the mean; σ\sigmaσ (sigma) is its width, the standard deviation, and σ2\sigma^2σ2 the variance.
  • (x−μ)2(x - \mu)^2(x−μ)2 is the squared distance from the centre; dividing by 2σ22\sigma^22σ2 measures that distance in units of the width.
  • exp⁡(u)=eu\exp(u) = e^uexp(u)=eu. With a minus sign in front, the density is largest at x=μx = \mux=μ and falls off quickly with distance.
  • 1σ2π\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}σ2π​1​ is the constant that makes the total area under the curve equal to 1.

In one sentence: the Gaussian density is a bell centred at μ\muμ with width σ\sigmaσ, falling off with the squared distance from the centre. At the centre with σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1, the density is 1/2π≈0.3991/\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 0.3991/2π​≈0.399.

Take the log of the density, add over the sample, and the log-likelihood is

L(S;μ,σ)=−12σ2∑i=1m(xi−μ)2−mlog⁡(σ2π).L(S; \mu, \sigma) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \mu)^2 - m\log\left(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\right).L(S;μ,σ)=−2σ21​i=1∑m​(xi​−μ)2−mlog(σ2π​).
  • log⁡\loglog undoes exp⁡\expexp, so each example contributes −(xi−μ)2/(2σ2)-(x_i - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)−(xi​−μ)2/(2σ2), plus log⁡\loglog of the constant, which is −log⁡(σ2π)-\log(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})−log(σ2π​).
  • The mmm copies of that constant add up to the last term.
  • The first term is a penalty for points far from μ\muμ; the second is a penalty for a wide bell.

In one sentence: a Gaussian explains the data well when the points are close to its centre and its bell is no wider than it needs to be. Five keep messages with length scores 3.1, 2.4, 4.0, 3.5 and 2.0 give, for μ=3\mu = 3μ=3 and σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1, the log-likelihood −12(0.01+0.36+1+0.25+1)−5log⁡2π=−1.31−4.595=−5.905-\frac12(0.01 + 0.36 + 1 + 0.25 + 1) - 5\log\sqrt{2\pi} = -1.31 - 4.595 = -5.905−21​(0.01+0.36+1+0.25+1)−5log2π​=−1.31−4.595=−5.905.

Proposition (the Gaussian MLE). If not all xix_ixi​ are equal, the maximum likelihood estimates are the sample mean and the root of the average squared deviation:

μ^=1m∑i=1mxi,σ^=1m∑i=1m(xi−μ^)2.\hat\mu = \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i, \qquad \hat\sigma = \sqrt{\frac1m \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \hat\mu)^2}.μ^​=m1​i=1∑m​xi​,σ^=m1​i=1∑m​(xi​−μ^​)2​.

Here μ^\hat\muμ^​ is the plain average, and σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2 the average squared distance from it. In one sentence: fit the bell’s centre at the average and its width at the typical distance from the average. For the five scores, μ^=15/5=3.0\hat\mu = 15/5 = 3.0μ^​=15/5=3.0 and σ^2=2.62/5=0.524\hat\sigma^2 = 2.62/5 = 0.524σ^2=2.62/5=0.524, so σ^≈0.724\hat\sigma \approx 0.724σ^≈0.724.

Proof. Two steps: first the centre for any fixed width, then the width.

Fix σ\sigmaσ. Only the first term depends on μ\muμ, and it is largest when ∑i(xi−μ)2\sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2∑i​(xi​−μ)2 is smallest. Write xi−μ=(xi−μ^)+(μ^−μ)x_i - \mu = (x_i - \hat\mu) + (\hat\mu - \mu)xi​−μ=(xi​−μ^​)+(μ^​−μ) and square:

∑i=1m(xi−μ)2=∑i=1m(xi−μ^)2+2(μ^−μ)∑i=1m(xi−μ^)+m(μ^−μ)2.\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \mu)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \hat\mu)^2 + 2(\hat\mu - \mu)\sum_{i=1}^{m}(x_i - \hat\mu) + m(\hat\mu - \mu)^2.i=1∑m​(xi​−μ)2=i=1∑m​(xi​−μ^​)2+2(μ^​−μ)i=1∑m​(xi​−μ^​)+m(μ^​−μ)2.

The middle sum is ∑ixi−mμ^=0\sum_i x_i - m\hat\mu = 0∑i​xi​−mμ^​=0, by the definition of μ^\hat\muμ^​. So the total squared distance to any centre μ\muμ is the total squared distance to the average plus mmm times the squared gap between μ\muμ and the average. It is smallest exactly at μ=μ^\mu = \hat\muμ=μ^​, whatever σ\sigmaσ is. (With the five scores and μ=3.5\mu = 3.5μ=3.5: 2.62+5⋅0.25=3.872.62 + 5 \cdot 0.25 = 3.872.62+5⋅0.25=3.87.)

Now put μ=μ^\mu = \hat\muμ=μ^​ and write A=∑i(xi−μ^)2A = \sum_i (x_i - \hat\mu)^2A=∑i​(xi​−μ^​)2, which is positive because not all xix_ixi​ are equal. The log-likelihood as a function of σ>0\sigma > 0σ>0 is g(σ)=−A/(2σ2)−mlog⁡σ−mlog⁡2πg(\sigma) = -A/(2\sigma^2) - m\log\sigma - m\log\sqrt{2\pi}g(σ)=−A/(2σ2)−mlogσ−mlog2π​, with derivative

g′(σ)=Aσ3−mσ=A−mσ2σ3.g'(\sigma) = \frac{A}{\sigma^3} - \frac{m}{\sigma} = \frac{A - m\sigma^2}{\sigma^3}.g′(σ)=σ3A​−σm​=σ3A−mσ2​.

The slope is positive while σ2\sigma^2σ2 is below A/mA/mA/m and negative after, so ggg climbs and then falls, and its maximum is at σ2=A/m\sigma^2 = A/mσ2=A/m, which is σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2. ■\blacksquare■

(Why the condition “not all equal”? If every xix_ixi​ is the same, A=0A = 0A=0 and g(σ)=−mlog⁡σ−constg(\sigma) = -m\log\sigma - \text{const}g(σ)=−mlogσ−const grows without limit as σ→0\sigma \to 0σ→0: an infinitely thin bell on a single point. There is no maximum. Hold on to this; it is the continuous cousin of our zero-probability bug.)

import math
xs = [3.1, 2.4, 4.0, 3.5, 2.0]
def L(mu, sigma):
    sq = sum((x - mu)**2 for x in xs)
    c = len(xs) * math.log(sigma * math.sqrt(2 * math.pi))
    return -sq / (2 * sigma**2) - c
mu_hat = sum(xs) / len(xs)
s_hat = math.sqrt(sum((x - mu_hat)**2 for x in xs) / len(xs))
print(round(L(3, 1), 3), mu_hat, round(s_hat, 3))
best = max(((L(mu_hat + a / 100, s_hat + b / 100), a, b)
            for a in range(-20, 21) for b in range(-20, 21)))
print(round(best[0], 3), best[1:])

It prints -5.905 3.0 0.724, then -5.479 (0, 0): around the formulas, nudging the centre or the width in any direction only lowers the log-likelihood.

One more property you will prove yourself at the end of the lesson. The centre estimate μ^\hat\muμ^​ is unbiased. The width estimate is not: on average, σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2 comes out a little too small. Maximum likelihood estimates are not always unbiased.

Maximum likelihood is ERM in disguise

Here is the surprise this lesson promised. Go back to lesson 3’s general setting: a loss function ℓ(h,z)\ell(h, z)ℓ(h,z) says how badly hypothesis hhh does on example zzz, the empirical risk is the average loss on the training sequence, and ERM, empirical risk minimization, returns the hypothesis with the smallest empirical risk.

Now let the “hypothesis” be a parameter θ\thetaθ and the example be an observation xxx. How badly does θ\thetaθ do on xxx? A natural answer is: by how surprised the model is to see xxx. If Pθ[x]P_\theta[x]Pθ​[x] is close to 1, the model expected it, and the loss should be near 0. If Pθ[x]P_\theta[x]Pθ​[x] is tiny, the model was badly wrong, and the loss should be large. The negative logarithm does exactly this. Under θ=0.75\theta = 0.75θ=0.75 for “prize”, a message with “prize” costs −log⁡0.75=0.288-\log 0.75 = 0.288−log0.75=0.288, and a message without it costs −log⁡0.25=1.386-\log 0.25 = 1.386−log0.25=1.386.

Definition (log loss). The log loss of parameter θ\thetaθ on observation xxx is

ℓ(θ,x)=−log⁡Pθ[x].\ell(\theta, x) = -\log P_\theta[x].ℓ(θ,x)=−logPθ​[x].
  • ℓ\ellℓ is the loss function of lesson 3, now with a parameter in the hypothesis slot and an observation (no label) in the example slot.
  • Pθ[x]P_\theta[x]Pθ​[x] is the probability (or density) the model gives to what actually happened.
  • The minus sign turns the log, which is negative for probabilities below 1, into a nonnegative cost.

In one sentence: the log loss is how surprised the model was by what it saw. A probability of 1 costs 0; a probability of 0 costs −log⁡0=+∞-\log 0 = +\infty−log0=+∞. Because we use the natural logarithm, log losses are measured in units called nats; with base-2 logarithms they would be bits, as in lesson 18.

Since the empirical risk with this loss is 1m∑i(−log⁡Pθ[xi])=−1mL(S;θ)\frac1m\sum_i(-\log P_\theta[x_i]) = -\frac1m L(S;\theta)m1​∑i​(−logPθ​[xi​])=−m1​L(S;θ), minimizing one is maximizing the other:

argmin⁡θ∑i=1m(−log⁡Pθ[xi])=argmax⁡θ∑i=1mlog⁡Pθ[xi].\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(-\log P_\theta[x_i]\right) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P_\theta[x_i].θargmin​i=1∑m​(−logPθ​[xi​])=θargmax​i=1∑m​logPθ​[xi​].
  • argmin⁡\operatorname*{argmin}argmin is where the left sum, mmm times the empirical risk, is smallest; argmax⁡\operatorname*{argmax}argmax is where the right sum, the log-likelihood, is largest. One is the negative of the other.

In one sentence: the maximum likelihood estimator is exactly ERM with the log loss. For “prize”, the empirical risk at θ=0.75\theta = 0.75θ=0.75 is 2.249/4=0.5622.249/4 = 0.5622.249/4=0.562, and no other θ\thetaθ does better. You met one instance of this in lesson 9: logistic regression is maximum likelihood for a model of the label given the message.

import math
S = [1, 0, 1, 1]
def loss(th, x):
    return -math.log(th if x == 1 else 1 - th)
def risk_S(th):
    return sum(loss(th, x) for x in S) / len(S)
print(round(loss(0.75, 1), 3), round(loss(0.75, 0), 3))
grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(1, 1000)]
best = min(grid, key=risk_S)
print(best, round(risk_S(best), 3))

It prints 0.288 1.386, then 0.75 0.562.

The true risk. ERM is only as good as the true risk it is chasing, so let’s compute it. Suppose the observations really come from some distribution PPP, which need not be of the form PθP_\thetaPθ​ at all. The true risk of θ\thetaθ is its expected log loss on a fresh observation, and it splits into two pieces. First the idea, with numbers. Say the word truly appears with probability 0.3, and the model uses θ=0.5\theta = 0.5θ=0.5. Then the expected surprise is 0.3⋅(−log⁡0.5)+0.7⋅(−log⁡0.5)=0.6930.3 \cdot (-\log 0.5) + 0.7 \cdot (-\log 0.5) = 0.6930.3⋅(−log0.5)+0.7⋅(−log0.5)=0.693. Even the perfect model, θ=0.3\theta = 0.3θ=0.3, would be surprised on average by −0.3log⁡0.3−0.7log⁡0.7=0.611-0.3\log 0.3 - 0.7\log 0.7 = 0.611−0.3log0.3−0.7log0.7=0.611: the data is random, and some surprise is unavoidable. The difference, 0.0820.0820.082, is the price of using the wrong parameter. In symbols:

Ex∼P[ℓ(θ,x)]=∑xP[x]log⁡P[x]Pθ[x]+∑xP[x]log⁡1P[x]=DRE(P ∥ Pθ)+H(P).\mathbb E_{x \sim P}\left[\ell(\theta, x)\right] = \sum_x P[x]\log\frac{P[x]}{P_\theta[x]} + \sum_x P[x]\log\frac{1}{P[x]} = D_{\mathrm{RE}}(P \,\|\, P_\theta) + H(P).Ex∼P​[ℓ(θ,x)]=x∑​P[x]logPθ​[x]P[x]​+x∑​P[x]logP[x]1​=DRE​(P∥Pθ​)+H(P).
  • x∼Px \sim Px∼P reads “xxx is drawn from PPP”, and Ex∼P\mathbb E_{x \sim P}Ex∼P​ averages over that draw: each possible xxx weighted by its true probability P[x]P[x]P[x].
  • The first equality adds and subtracts log⁡P[x]\log P[x]logP[x] inside −log⁡Pθ[x]-\log P_\theta[x]−logPθ​[x]: −log⁡Pθ[x]=log⁡P[x]Pθ[x]+log⁡1P[x]-\log P_\theta[x] = \log\frac{P[x]}{P_\theta[x]} + \log\frac{1}{P[x]}−logPθ​[x]=logPθ​[x]P[x]​+logP[x]1​.
  • H(P)=∑xP[x]log⁡1P[x]H(P) = \sum_x P[x]\log\frac{1}{P[x]}H(P)=∑x​P[x]logP[x]1​ is the entropy of PPP: the average surprise of the true distribution about itself. It does not depend on θ\thetaθ. (Lesson 18 used the same quantity in base 2 to choose splits.)
  • DRE(P∥Pθ)=∑xP[x]log⁡P[x]Pθ[x]D_{\mathrm{RE}}(P \| P_\theta) = \sum_x P[x]\log\frac{P[x]}{P_\theta[x]}DRE​(P∥Pθ​)=∑x​P[x]logPθ​[x]P[x]​ is the relative entropy of PPP to PθP_\thetaPθ​, also called the Kullback–Leibler divergence: the extra surprise from believing PθP_\thetaPθ​ when the truth is PPP. The double bar ∥\|∥ only separates its two arguments, and the order matters.
  • Terms with P[x]=0P[x] = 0P[x]=0 are left out of both sums: an outcome that never happens costs nothing on average.

In one sentence: the true risk of a parameter is the unavoidable randomness of the data plus the extra surprise caused by the model being wrong. In the example, 0.693=0.611+0.0820.693 = 0.611 + 0.0820.693=0.611+0.082.

The entropy is the floor nobody can go below, as long as the relative entropy is never negative. It isn’t:

Proposition (relative entropy is nonnegative). For distributions PPP and QQQ on a finite set, DRE(P∥Q)≥0D_{\mathrm{RE}}(P\|Q) \ge 0DRE​(P∥Q)≥0, with equality exactly when Q=PQ = PQ=P.

Proof. The engine is a one-line inequality: log⁡t≤t−1\log t \le t - 1logt≤t−1 for every t>0t > 0t>0, with equality only at t=1t = 1t=1. To see it, let g(t)=t−1−log⁡tg(t) = t - 1 - \log tg(t)=t−1−logt. Its derivative 1−1/t1 - 1/t1−1/t is negative for t<1t < 1t<1 and positive for t>1t > 1t>1, so ggg falls to its minimum at t=1t = 1t=1, where g(1)=0g(1) = 0g(1)=0, and is positive everywhere else.

Now sum over the outcomes with P[x]>0P[x] > 0P[x]>0. If Q[x]=0Q[x] = 0Q[x]=0 for one of them, the term log⁡(P[x]/Q[x])\log(P[x]/Q[x])log(P[x]/Q[x]) is +∞+\infty+∞, and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise apply the inequality with t=Q[x]/P[x]t = Q[x]/P[x]t=Q[x]/P[x]:

−DRE(P∥Q)=∑x:P[x]>0P[x]log⁡Q[x]P[x]≤∑x:P[x]>0P[x](Q[x]P[x]−1)=∑x:P[x]>0Q[x]−1≤0.-D_{\mathrm{RE}}(P\|Q) = \sum_{x : P[x] > 0} P[x]\log\frac{Q[x]}{P[x]} \le \sum_{x : P[x] > 0} P[x]\left(\frac{Q[x]}{P[x]} - 1\right) = \sum_{x : P[x] > 0} Q[x] - 1 \le 0.−DRE​(P∥Q)=x:P[x]>0∑​P[x]logP[x]Q[x]​≤x:P[x]>0∑​P[x](P[x]Q[x]​−1)=x:P[x]>0∑​Q[x]−1≤0.
  • The colon in ∑x:P[x]>0\sum_{x : P[x] > 0}∑x:P[x]>0​ reads “such that”: add over the outcomes xxx such that P[x]>0P[x] > 0P[x]>0.
  • The middle step multiplies out: P[x]⋅Q[x]/P[x]=Q[x]P[x] \cdot Q[x]/P[x] = Q[x]P[x]⋅Q[x]/P[x]=Q[x], and the P[x]P[x]P[x] add up to 1.
  • The last step holds because QQQ’s total over some outcomes is at most its total over all, which is 1.

In one sentence: minus the relative entropy is at most QQQ’s total mass on the outcomes PPP can produce, minus 1, which is never positive. Equality needs both inequalities to be equalities: Q[x]/P[x]=1Q[x]/P[x] = 1Q[x]/P[x]=1 wherever P[x]>0P[x] > 0P[x]>0, and QQQ putting no mass elsewhere. That is Q=PQ = PQ=P. ■\blacksquare■

import math
P = {1: 0.3, 0: 0.7}
def Q(th):
    return {1: th, 0: 1 - th}
def risk(th):
    return sum(-P[x] * math.log(Q(th)[x]) for x in P)
H = sum(P[x] * math.log(1 / P[x]) for x in P)
def D(th):
    return sum(P[x] * math.log(P[x] / Q(th)[x]) for x in P)
for th in (0.1, 0.3, 0.5):
    print(th, round(risk(th), 3), round(H, 3), round(D(th), 3))

It prints 0.1 0.765 0.611 0.154, 0.3 0.611 0.611 0.0 and 0.5 0.693 0.611 0.082: in every row the risk is the entropy plus the relative entropy, and the relative entropy vanishes only at the truth.

So the true risk is smallest when Pθ=PP_\theta = PPθ​=P. If the data really has the assumed parametric form, the right parameter brings the risk down to the entropy. If it does not, even the best parameter pays a relative entropy forever, no matter how much data you collect. That is the inductive bias of a generative model, in the sense of lesson 1: the parametric form is a hypothesis class, chosen before seeing any data, and it can miss the truth.

[diagram:logloss: built on the lesson page]

How well does maximum likelihood generalize?

Lesson 2 asked of every learner: trained on a finite training sequence, how good is its true risk? For a generative model the natural yardstick is the one we just built, the expected log loss. Since the entropy is a floor nobody can beat, what matters is the excess risk: the true risk of the estimate minus the true risk of the best parameter. Let’s compute it for two models, one where maximum likelihood behaves beautifully and one where it fails outright.

A well-behaved case: the centre of a bell. Suppose the length scores of keep messages really are Gaussian with width σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1 and an unknown centre μ⋆\mu^\starμ⋆ (the star marks the true value). We estimate the centre by μ^\hat\muμ^​, the average. If the estimate is off by 0.2, how much extra surprise does that cost on a fresh message? Intuition says something like the square of the miss, and the exact answer is 12⋅0.22=0.02\tfrac12 \cdot 0.2^2 = 0.0221​⋅0.22=0.02. Here is the calculation, with ℓ(μ,x)=−log⁡Pμ(x)\ell(\mu, x) = -\log P_\mu(x)ℓ(μ,x)=−logPμ​(x) the log loss of the unit-width Gaussian:

Ex∼N(μ⋆,1)[ℓ(μ^,x)−ℓ(μ⋆,x)]=E[−12(x−μ⋆)2+12(x−μ^)2]=E[x(μ⋆−μ^)+12μ^2−12(μ⋆)2]=μ⋆(μ⋆−μ^)+12μ^2−12(μ⋆)2=12(μ^−μ⋆)2.\begin{aligned} \mathbb E_{x \sim N(\mu^\star, 1)}\left[\ell(\hat\mu, x) - \ell(\mu^\star, x)\right] &= \mathbb E\left[-\tfrac12 (x - \mu^\star)^2 + \tfrac12 (x - \hat\mu)^2\right] \\ &= \mathbb E\left[x(\mu^\star - \hat\mu) + \tfrac12\hat\mu^2 - \tfrac12(\mu^\star)^2\right] \\ &= \mu^\star(\mu^\star - \hat\mu) + \tfrac12\hat\mu^2 - \tfrac12(\mu^\star)^2 = \tfrac12(\hat\mu - \mu^\star)^2. \end{aligned}Ex∼N(μ⋆,1)​[ℓ(μ^​,x)−ℓ(μ⋆,x)]​=E[−21​(x−μ⋆)2+21​(x−μ^​)2]=E[x(μ⋆−μ^​)+21​μ^​2−21​(μ⋆)2]=μ⋆(μ⋆−μ^​)+21​μ^​2−21​(μ⋆)2=21​(μ^​−μ⋆)2.​
  • N(μ⋆,1)N(\mu^\star, 1)N(μ⋆,1) is the Gaussian with centre μ⋆\mu^\starμ⋆ and width 1, and x∼N(μ⋆,1)x \sim N(\mu^\star, 1)x∼N(μ⋆,1) is a fresh score drawn from it. The estimate μ^\hat\muμ^​ is held fixed: it was computed from the training sequence, and the fresh xxx is independent of it.
  • First line: ℓ(μ^,x)−ℓ(μ⋆,x)=log⁡Pμ⋆(x)−log⁡Pμ^(x)\ell(\hat\mu, x) - \ell(\mu^\star, x) = \log P_{\mu^\star}(x) - \log P_{\hat\mu}(x)ℓ(μ^​,x)−ℓ(μ⋆,x)=logPμ⋆​(x)−logPμ^​​(x). Both densities have the same constant 12π\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}2π​1​, which cancels, leaving the two exponents.
  • Second line: expand both squares. The x2x^2x2 terms cancel, −12(−2xμ⋆)+12(−2xμ^)=x(μ⋆−μ^)-\tfrac12(-2x\mu^\star) + \tfrac12(-2x\hat\mu) = x(\mu^\star - \hat\mu)−21​(−2xμ⋆)+21​(−2xμ^​)=x(μ⋆−μ^​), and the constants are 12μ^2−12(μ⋆)2\tfrac12\hat\mu^2 - \tfrac12(\mu^\star)^221​μ^​2−21​(μ⋆)2.
  • Third line: the only random thing left is xxx, and E[x]=μ⋆\mathbb E[x] = \mu^\starE[x]=μ⋆. Collect: 12μ^2−μ^μ⋆+12(μ⋆)2\tfrac12\hat\mu^2 - \hat\mu\mu^\star + \tfrac12(\mu^\star)^221​μ^​2−μ^​μ⋆+21​(μ⋆)2 is 12(μ^−μ⋆)2\tfrac12(\hat\mu - \mu^\star)^221​(μ^​−μ⋆)2.

In one sentence: using a centre that is off by some amount costs, on every fresh message on average, half the square of that amount. And how far off is μ^\hat\muμ^​? It is an average of mmm independent scores of variance 1, and lesson 4 showed that such an average has variance 1/m1/m1/m. Since μ^\hat\muμ^​ is unbiased, its variance is E[(μ^−μ⋆)2]\mathbb E[(\hat\mu - \mu^\star)^2]E[(μ^​−μ⋆)2], so the expected excess risk is exactly 1/(2m)1/(2m)1/(2m). Chebyshev’s inequality from lesson 4 says a variable lands at least aaa from its mean with probability at most its variance over a2a^2a2; with a2=1/(mδ)a^2 = 1/(m\delta)a2=1/(mδ) it gives P[(μ^−μ⋆)2≥1/(mδ)]≤δ\mathbb P[(\hat\mu - \mu^\star)^2 \ge 1/(m\delta)] \le \deltaP[(μ^​−μ⋆)2≥1/(mδ)]≤δ, so with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ the excess risk is below 1/(2mδ)1/(2m\delta)1/(2mδ). Ten messages give an expected excess of 0.050.050.05.

import random
rng, mu_star, m, runs = random.Random(1), 3.0, 10, 20000
total = 0.0
for _ in range(runs):
    mu_hat = sum(rng.gauss(mu_star, 1) for _ in range(m)) / m
    total += 0.5 * (mu_hat - mu_star)**2
print(round(total / runs, 3), 1 / (2 * m))

It prints 0.051 0.05: twenty thousand simulated training sequences land on 1/(2m)1/(2m)1/(2m).

A failing case: a rare word. Now the yes/no model, for a word that junk messages contain with a small probability θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆. Say “winner” is in one junk message out of 500, so θ⋆=0.002\theta^\star = 0.002θ⋆=0.002, and you have m=200m = 200m=200 junk messages. What is the chance that “winner” appears in none of them? Each message misses it with probability 0.998, independently, so the chance is 0.998200≈0.670.998^{200} \approx 0.670.998200≈0.67. Two times out of three, maximum likelihood sets θ^=0\hat\theta = 0θ^=0.

And then the true risk is infinite. The next junk message contains “winner” with probability θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆, and when it does, the log loss is −log⁡θ^=−log⁡0=+∞-\log \hat\theta = -\log 0 = +\infty−logθ^=−log0=+∞:

Ex∼θ⋆[ℓ(θ^,x)]=θ⋆log⁡1θ^+(1−θ⋆)log⁡11−θ^=θ⋆log⁡10=∞.\mathbb E_{x \sim \theta^\star}\left[\ell(\hat\theta, x)\right] = \theta^\star \log\frac{1}{\hat\theta} + (1 - \theta^\star)\log\frac{1}{1 - \hat\theta} = \theta^\star \log\frac10 = \infty.Ex∼θ⋆​[ℓ(θ^,x)]=θ⋆logθ^1​+(1−θ⋆)log1−θ^1​=θ⋆log01​=∞.
  • x∼θ⋆x \sim \theta^\starx∼θ⋆ is shorthand for “xxx is drawn from the Bernoulli distribution with parameter θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆”.
  • The two terms are the two possible observations, each weighted by its true probability: a 1 with probability θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆, costing log⁡(1/θ^)\log(1/\hat\theta)log(1/θ^), and a 0 with probability 1−θ⋆1 - \theta^\star1−θ⋆, costing log⁡(1/(1−θ^))\log(1/(1 - \hat\theta))log(1/(1−θ^)).
  • With θ^=0\hat\theta = 0θ^=0, the second term is log⁡1=0\log 1 = 0log1=0, and the first is a positive number times log⁡(1/0)=+∞\log(1/0) = +\inftylog(1/0)=+∞.

In one sentence: an estimate of exactly 0 for something that does happen makes the expected surprise infinite. It does not matter that θ^=0\hat\theta = 0θ^=0 is within 0.002 of the truth, a superb estimate by Hoeffding’s standards. The log loss magnifies errors near 0 without limit.

How often does this happen? The chance that all mmm observations are 0 is (1−θ⋆)m(1 - \theta^\star)^m(1−θ⋆)m. A clean lower bound: for 0≤θ⋆≤1/20 \le \theta^\star \le 1/20≤θ⋆≤1/2,

(1−θ⋆)m≥e−2θ⋆m.(1 - \theta^\star)^m \ge e^{-2\theta^\star m}.(1−θ⋆)m≥e−2θ⋆m.
  • θ⋆m\theta^\star mθ⋆m is the expected number of messages, out of mmm, that contain the word.
  • e−2θ⋆me^{-2\theta^\star m}e−2θ⋆m is easier to reason about than the power: it says the chance shrinks exponentially in the number of examples, at rate 2θ⋆2\theta^\star2θ⋆.

In one sentence: the chance of never seeing a rare word is at least eee to the minus twice the expected number of times you would see it. For “winner”, e−0.8≈0.449e^{-0.8} \approx 0.449e−0.8≈0.449, safely below the true 0.67. To prove it, write θ\thetaθ for θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆ and take logs: we need mlog⁡(1−θ)≥−2θmm\log(1 - \theta) \ge -2\theta mmlog(1−θ)≥−2θm, so it is enough that h(θ)=log⁡(1−θ)+2θ≥0h(\theta) = \log(1 - \theta) + 2\theta \ge 0h(θ)=log(1−θ)+2θ≥0. At θ=0\theta = 0θ=0, h(0)=0h(0) = 0h(0)=0, and its derivative −1/(1−θ)+2-1/(1 - \theta) + 2−1/(1−θ)+2 is nonnegative while 1−θ≥1/21 - \theta \ge 1/21−θ≥1/2, so hhh only grows on [0,1/2][0, 1/2][0,1/2].

Now ask when the bound is at least a half: e−2θ⋆m≥1/2e^{-2\theta^\star m} \ge 1/2e−2θ⋆m≥1/2 exactly when m≤log⁡2/(2θ⋆)m \le \log 2/(2\theta^\star)m≤log2/(2θ⋆). Whenever the training sequence has at most log⁡2/(2θ⋆)\log 2/(2\theta^\star)log2/(2θ⋆) examples, maximum likelihood has infinite true risk with probability at least one half. For “winner”, that is any mmm up to 173.

import math
theta, m = 0.002, 200
p_zero = (1 - theta)**m
print(round(p_zero, 3), round(math.exp(-2 * theta * m), 3))
print(math.floor(math.log(2) / (2 * theta)))
print(round((1 - theta)**173, 3))

It prints 0.67 0.449, then 173 and 0.707: at 173 examples the all-zero chance is still 71%.

This is Ines’s bug, now as a theorem. A dictionary has thousands of rare words. For each one, the counts say 0 with substantial probability, and each such 0 is a factor that can wipe out a whole producer’s probability. Maximum likelihood overfits, in exactly the sense of lesson 2: it fits the training sequence perfectly (it makes the observed data as likely as possible) while its true risk is as bad as it can be.

[diagram:zero: built on the lesson page]

The fix: pseudo-counts

Lesson 13 cured overfitting with a regularizer, a penalty that pulls the learner away from extreme answers. Let’s do the same here, in the most down-to-earth way possible. Before counting, pretend you have already seen α\alphaα junk messages that contain the word and α\alphaα that do not. These imaginary messages are pseudo-counts. With α=1\alpha = 1α=1, the estimate for “winner” in the four junk messages becomes (0+1)/(4+2)=1/6(0 + 1)/(4 + 2) = 1/6(0+1)/(4+2)=1/6 instead of 0, and the estimate for “free” becomes (3+1)/6=2/3(3 + 1)/6 = 2/3(3+1)/6=2/3 instead of 3/43/43/4. No word can ever get an estimate of 0 or 1 again.

Definition (the add-α\alphaα estimator). For α≥0\alpha \ge 0α≥0 and a training sequence with kkk ones among mmm observations,

θ^α=k+αm+2α.\hat\theta_\alpha = \frac{k + \alpha}{m + 2\alpha}.θ^α​=m+2αk+α​.
  • k+αk + \alphak+α is the number of ones, real and imaginary; m+2αm + 2\alpham+2α is the number of observations, real and imaginary.
  • α=0\alpha = 0α=0 gives back maximum likelihood, k/mk/mk/m. α=1\alpha = 1α=1 is called add-one smoothing, or Laplace’s rule.
  • Whatever the data, θ^α\hat\theta_\alphaθ^α​ lies between α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α) (no ones at all) and (m+α)/(m+2α)(m + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)(m+α)/(m+2α) (all ones).

In one sentence: estimate the frequency as if you had also seen α\alphaα imaginary examples of each kind. With m=4m = 4m=4, k=0k = 0k=0, α=1\alpha = 1α=1: 1/6≈0.1671/6 \approx 0.1671/6≈0.167.

This is regularized maximum likelihood, not just a hack. Add to the empirical log loss a penalty that charges the parameter for being near 0 or near 1:

1m∑i=1mlog⁡1Pθ[xi]+αm(log⁡1θ+log⁡11−θ).\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\frac{1}{P_\theta[x_i]} + \frac{\alpha}{m}\left(\log\frac1\theta + \log\frac{1}{1-\theta}\right).m1​i=1∑m​logPθ​[xi​]1​+mα​(logθ1​+log1−θ1​).
  • The first part is the empirical risk with the log loss, as before.
  • The penalty log⁡(1/θ)+log⁡(1/(1−θ))\log(1/\theta) + \log(1/(1-\theta))log(1/θ)+log(1/(1−θ)) is exactly the log loss of θ\thetaθ on two imaginary observations, one 1 and one 0; it is huge near either end.
  • The weight α/m\alpha/mα/m says how much the penalty counts, relative to one real example.

In one sentence: the regularized objective is the average log loss on the real examples plus α\alphaα imaginary ones and α\alphaα imaginary zeros. Multiply it by mmm: you get −(k+α)log⁡θ−(m−k+α)log⁡(1−θ)-(k + \alpha)\log\theta - (m - k + \alpha)\log(1 - \theta)−(k+α)logθ−(m−k+α)log(1−θ), the negative log-likelihood of a sequence with k+αk + \alphak+α ones and m−k+αm - k + \alpham−k+α zeros. For α>0\alpha > 0α>0 both counts are positive, and the proof of the Bernoulli MLE (which used only that the counts are positive numbers, never that they are whole) puts the unique minimizer at (k+α)/(m+2α)(k + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)(k+α)/(m+2α). So the add-α\alphaα estimator is ERM with a regularizer, the pattern of lesson 13.

import math
k, m, alpha = 0, 4, 1
def objective(th):
    real = -(k * math.log(th) + (m - k) * math.log(1 - th))
    fake = alpha * (math.log(1 / th) + math.log(1 / (1 - th)))
    return (real + fake) / m
grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(1, 1000)]
theta_alpha = (k + alpha) / (m + 2 * alpha)
print(min(grid, key=objective), round(theta_alpha, 3))

It prints 0.167 0.167.

What does this buy? Here is the guarantee, the heart of the fix. It has three parts: the estimate stays accurate, the expected excess risk becomes finite, and without pseudo-counts it cannot be.

Theorem (the pseudo-count guarantee). Let x1,…,xmx_1, \dots, x_mx1​,…,xm​ be i.i.d. Bernoulli with parameter θ⋆∈[0,1]\theta^\star \in [0, 1]θ⋆∈[0,1], and let θ^=θ^α\hat\theta = \hat\theta_\alphaθ^=θ^α​. Write the excess risk of a parameter qqq as Δ(q)=Ex∼θ⋆[ℓ(q,x)]−Ex∼θ⋆[ℓ(θ⋆,x)]\Delta(q) = \mathbb E_{x \sim \theta^\star}[\ell(q, x)] - \mathbb E_{x \sim \theta^\star}[\ell(\theta^\star, x)]Δ(q)=Ex∼θ⋆​[ℓ(q,x)]−Ex∼θ⋆​[ℓ(θ⋆,x)].

(a) For every α≥0\alpha \ge 0α≥0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ,

∣θ^−θ⋆∣≤log⁡(2/δ)2m+αm+2α.|\hat\theta - \theta^\star| \le \sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}} + \frac{\alpha}{m + 2\alpha}.∣θ^−θ⋆∣≤2mlog(2/δ)​​+m+2αα​.

(b) For every α>0\alpha > 0α>0,

ES[Δ(θ^)]≤mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)+α2α(m+α)≤m/4+α2α(m+α).\mathbb E_S\left[\Delta(\hat\theta)\right] \le \frac{m\theta^\star(1-\theta^\star) + \alpha^2}{\alpha(m + \alpha)} \le \frac{m/4 + \alpha^2}{\alpha(m + \alpha)}.ES​[Δ(θ^)]≤α(m+α)mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)+α2​≤α(m+α)m/4+α2​.

(c) For α=0\alpha = 0α=0 and 0<θ⋆<10 < \theta^\star < 10<θ⋆<1, PS[Δ(θ^)=∞]≥(1−θ⋆)m>0\mathbb P_S[\Delta(\hat\theta) = \infty] \ge (1 - \theta^\star)^m > 0PS​[Δ(θ^)=∞]≥(1−θ⋆)m>0, so ES[Δ(θ^)]=∞\mathbb E_S[\Delta(\hat\theta)] = \inftyES​[Δ(θ^)]=∞.

Let’s read the three formulas before proving them.

  • In (a), the first term is Hoeffding’s accuracy from before; the second, α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α), is the most the imaginary examples can drag the estimate. The estimate is within the usual Hoeffding distance of the truth, plus a small pull from the pseudo-counts that fades as mmm grows. With m=600m = 600m=600, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, α=1\alpha = 1α=1: 0.0554+0.0017=0.05710.0554 + 0.0017 = 0.05710.0554+0.0017=0.0571.
  • In (b), ES\mathbb E_SES​ averages over the random training sequence, and Δ(θ^)\Delta(\hat\theta)Δ(θ^) is the extra expected log loss of the estimate on a fresh observation. The numerator grows with how random the word is (θ⋆(1−θ⋆)\theta^\star(1-\theta^\star)θ⋆(1−θ⋆) is largest at 1/21/21/2, where it equals 1/41/41/4, which gives the second bound); the denominator grows with α\alphaα. With pseudo-counts, the expected excess risk is finite for every word, however rare, and we can say how big it can be. For “winner” (θ⋆=0.002\theta^\star = 0.002θ⋆=0.002, m=200m = 200m=200, α=1\alpha = 1α=1): (0.399+1)/201≈0.007(0.399 + 1)/201 \approx 0.007(0.399+1)/201≈0.007.
  • In (c), PS\mathbb P_SPS​ is the probability over the training sequence. Without pseudo-counts, every word that is neither impossible nor certain has infinite expected excess risk.

Proof of (a). Write xˉ=k/m\bar x = k/mxˉ=k/m for the plain average, so θ^=(mxˉ+α)/(m+2α)\hat\theta = (m\bar x + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)θ^=(mxˉ+α)/(m+2α). The trick is to compare θ^\hat\thetaθ^ with its own expectation, then the expectation with the truth.

The expectation: E[k]=mθ⋆\mathbb E[k] = m\theta^\starE[k]=mθ⋆, so E[θ^]=(mθ⋆+α)/(m+2α)\mathbb E[\hat\theta] = (m\theta^\star + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)E[θ^]=(mθ⋆+α)/(m+2α). Its distance from the truth, the bias, is

E[θ^]−θ⋆=mθ⋆+α−(m+2α)θ⋆m+2α=α(1−2θ⋆)m+2α,\mathbb E[\hat\theta] - \theta^\star = \frac{m\theta^\star + \alpha - (m + 2\alpha)\theta^\star}{m + 2\alpha} = \frac{\alpha(1 - 2\theta^\star)}{m + 2\alpha},E[θ^]−θ⋆=m+2αmθ⋆+α−(m+2α)θ⋆​=m+2αα(1−2θ⋆)​,

and since ∣1−2θ⋆∣≤1|1 - 2\theta^\star| \le 1∣1−2θ⋆∣≤1, its size is at most α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α). The pseudo-counts pull the average estimate toward 1/21/21/2, by at most α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α). For “winner” with m=200m = 200m=200, α=1\alpha = 1α=1: 0.996/202≈0.00490.996/202 \approx 0.00490.996/202≈0.0049.

The fluctuation: θ^−E[θ^]=mm+2α(xˉ−θ⋆)\hat\theta - \mathbb E[\hat\theta] = \frac{m}{m + 2\alpha}(\bar x - \theta^\star)θ^−E[θ^]=m+2αm​(xˉ−θ⋆), and the factor m/(m+2α)m/(m + 2\alpha)m/(m+2α) is at most 1, so ∣θ^−Eθ^∣≤∣xˉ−θ⋆∣|\hat\theta - \mathbb E\hat\theta| \le |\bar x - \theta^\star|∣θ^−Eθ^∣≤∣xˉ−θ⋆∣, which Hoeffding bounds by log⁡(2/δ)/(2m)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}log(2/δ)/(2m)​ with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ.

Put them together with the triangle inequality, ∣a+b∣≤∣a∣+∣b∣|a + b| \le |a| + |b|∣a+b∣≤∣a∣+∣b∣, applied to θ^−θ⋆=(θ^−Eθ^)+(Eθ^−θ⋆)\hat\theta - \theta^\star = (\hat\theta - \mathbb E\hat\theta) + (\mathbb E\hat\theta - \theta^\star)θ^−θ⋆=(θ^−Eθ^)+(Eθ^−θ⋆). ■\blacksquare■

Proof of (b). Three steps: the excess risk is a relative entropy, the relative entropy is at most a squared distance divided by q(1−q)q(1-q)q(1−q), and the pseudo-counts keep q(1−q)q(1-q)q(1−q) away from 0.

Step 1. By the decomposition of the previous section, the true risk of qqq is H+DRE(θ⋆∥q)H + D_{\mathrm{RE}}(\theta^\star\|q)H+DRE​(θ⋆∥q), and of θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆ itself it is H+0H + 0H+0. So Δ(q)=DRE(θ⋆∥q)\Delta(q) = D_{\mathrm{RE}}(\theta^\star \| q)Δ(q)=DRE​(θ⋆∥q), where for yes/no distributions we write the parameters in place of the distributions.

Step 2. Fix p=θ⋆p = \theta^\starp=θ⋆ and look at the true risk as a function of the parameter, f(q)=−plog⁡q−(1−p)log⁡(1−q)f(q) = -p\log q - (1-p)\log(1-q)f(q)=−plogq−(1−p)log(1−q) for 0<q<10 < q < 10<q<1. Its derivatives are

f′(q)=−pq+1−p1−q=q−pq(1−q),f′′(q)=pq2+1−p(1−q)2≥0.f'(q) = -\frac{p}{q} + \frac{1-p}{1-q} = \frac{q - p}{q(1-q)}, \qquad f''(q) = \frac{p}{q^2} + \frac{1-p}{(1-q)^2} \ge 0.f′(q)=−qp​+1−q1−p​=q(1−q)q−p​,f′′(q)=q2p​+(1−q)21−p​≥0.
  • Over a common denominator, the numerator of f′(q)f'(q)f′(q), −p(1−q)+(1−p)q-p(1 - q) + (1 - p)q−p(1−q)+(1−p)q, simplifies to q−pq - pq−p; f′′(q)f''(q)f′′(q) is a sum of nonnegative terms.

In one sentence: the true risk slopes toward the truth, and it curves upward everywhere. A function whose second derivative is nonnegative is convex, and lesson 12 showed that a differentiable convex function lies above each of its tangent lines: f(p)≥f(q)+f′(q)(p−q)f(p) \ge f(q) + f'(q)(p - q)f(p)≥f(q)+f′(q)(p−q). (If ppp is 0 or 1, fff is still defined there by continuity and the same holds.) Rearranged,

Δ(q)=f(q)−f(p)≤f′(q)(q−p)=(q−p)2q(1−q).\Delta(q) = f(q) - f(p) \le f'(q)(q - p) = \frac{(q - p)^2}{q(1 - q)}.Δ(q)=f(q)−f(p)≤f′(q)(q−p)=q(1−q)(q−p)2​.

The excess risk of a parameter is at most its squared distance from the truth, divided by q(1−q)q(1-q)q(1−q). For p=0.3p = 0.3p=0.3, q=0.5q = 0.5q=0.5: the excess is 0.0820.0820.082, and the bound is 0.04/0.25=0.160.04/0.25 = 0.160.04/0.25=0.16. Notice the denominator: near 0 or 1 it collapses, which is the whole story of the bug.

Step 3. With pseudo-counts, q=θ^q = \hat\thetaq=θ^ lies in the interval from a=α/(m+2α)a = \alpha/(m + 2\alpha)a=α/(m+2α) to 1−a1 - a1−a. The function t(1−t)t(1 - t)t(1−t) is a downward parabola, so on an interval it is smallest at an end, and both ends give a(1−a)=α(m+α)/(m+2α)2a(1-a) = \alpha(m + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)^2a(1−a)=α(m+α)/(m+2α)2. So, for every training sequence,

Δ(θ^)≤(θ^−θ⋆)2(m+2α)2α(m+α).\Delta(\hat\theta) \le \frac{(\hat\theta - \theta^\star)^2 (m + 2\alpha)^2}{\alpha(m + \alpha)}.Δ(θ^)≤α(m+α)(θ^−θ⋆)2(m+2α)2​.

Now average over SSS. The expected squared distance splits into variance plus squared bias: writing θ^−θ⋆=(θ^−Eθ^)+(Eθ^−θ⋆)\hat\theta - \theta^\star = (\hat\theta - \mathbb E\hat\theta) + (\mathbb E\hat\theta - \theta^\star)θ^−θ⋆=(θ^−Eθ^)+(Eθ^−θ⋆) and squaring, the cross term has expectation 0 because E[θ^−Eθ^]=0\mathbb E[\hat\theta - \mathbb E\hat\theta] = 0E[θ^−Eθ^]=0. The variance of θ^=(k+α)/(m+2α)\hat\theta = (k + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)θ^=(k+α)/(m+2α) is Var⁡[k]/(m+2α)2=mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)/(m+2α)2\operatorname{Var}[k]/(m + 2\alpha)^2 = m\theta^\star(1 - \theta^\star)/(m + 2\alpha)^2Var[k]/(m+2α)2=mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)/(m+2α)2, since kkk is a sum of mmm independent coins, variances of independent draws add (lesson 4), and each coin has variance E[x2]−(θ⋆)2=θ⋆−(θ⋆)2=θ⋆(1−θ⋆)\mathbb E[x^2] - (\theta^\star)^2 = \theta^\star - (\theta^\star)^2 = \theta^\star(1 - \theta^\star)E[x2]−(θ⋆)2=θ⋆−(θ⋆)2=θ⋆(1−θ⋆), because x2=xx^2 = xx2=x for a 0 or 1. The squared bias is α2(1−2θ⋆)2/(m+2α)2≤α2/(m+2α)2\alpha^2(1 - 2\theta^\star)^2/(m + 2\alpha)^2 \le \alpha^2/(m + 2\alpha)^2α2(1−2θ⋆)2/(m+2α)2≤α2/(m+2α)2. So

ES[(θ^−θ⋆)2]≤mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)+α2(m+2α)2,\mathbb E_S\left[(\hat\theta - \theta^\star)^2\right] \le \frac{m\theta^\star(1-\theta^\star) + \alpha^2}{(m + 2\alpha)^2},ES​[(θ^−θ⋆)2]≤(m+2α)2mθ⋆(1−θ⋆)+α2​,

and multiplying by (m+2α)2/(α(m+α))(m + 2\alpha)^2/(\alpha(m + \alpha))(m+2α)2/(α(m+α)) gives the first bound in (b). (For “winner”, the expected squared distance is at most 1.399/2022≈0.0000341.399/202^2 \approx 0.0000341.399/2022≈0.000034.) The second uses θ⋆(1−θ⋆)≤1/4\theta^\star(1 - \theta^\star) \le 1/4θ⋆(1−θ⋆)≤1/4. ■\blacksquare■

Proof of (c). With α=0\alpha = 0α=0, θ^=0\hat\theta = 0θ^=0 whenever all mmm observations are 0, which has probability (1−θ⋆)m(1 - \theta^\star)^m(1−θ⋆)m, positive because θ⋆<1\theta^\star < 1θ⋆<1. On that event the excess risk is infinite, as computed for “winner”, because θ⋆>0\theta^\star > 0θ⋆>0. An expectation that puts positive probability on +∞+\infty+∞ is +∞+\infty+∞. ■\blacksquare■

Let’s check (b) for “winner” by computing the expectation exactly, adding over every possible count kkk weighted by its binomial probability:

import math
def D(p, q):
    if q in (0, 1):
        return math.inf
    return (p * math.log(p / q)
            + (1 - p) * math.log((1 - p) / (1 - q)))
def expected_excess(p, m, a):
    w = [math.comb(m, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(m - k)
         for k in range(m + 1)]
    return sum(w[k] * D(p, (k + a) / (m + 2 * a))
               for k in range(m + 1) if w[k] > 0)
p, m = 0.002, 200
for a in (0, 1):
    top = m * p * (1 - p) + a * a
    bound = top / (a * (m + a)) if a else math.inf
    print(a, round(expected_excess(p, m, a), 4), round(bound, 4))

It prints 0 inf inf and 1 0.0026 0.007: no pseudo-counts, infinite risk; one pseudo-count each way, an expected excess of 0.0026 nats, safely under the bound of 0.007.

[diagram:pseudocounts: built on the lesson page]

There is a price, and (a) shows it. The pull α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α) is a bias toward 1/21/21/2. One pseudo-count is a whisper next to 600 real messages; a hundred pseudo-counts would drown a rare word’s real frequency. And (b) shows that too few pseudo-counts are dangerous in the other direction: as α\alphaα shrinks toward 0, the bound (m/4+α2)/(α(m+α))(m/4 + \alpha^2)/(\alpha(m + \alpha))(m/4+α2)/(α(m+α)) grows like 1/(4α)1/(4\alpha)1/(4α). Remember this when you fix the filter: the guarantee needs both halves.

A second road to the same place: Bayesian reasoning

Add-one smoothing has a second, independent justification, and it comes from a different philosophy of what a parameter is.

So far we have treated θ\thetaθ as a fixed number that we simply do not know. This is the frequentist view. The Bayesian view says: if we are uncertain about θ\thetaθ, let’s describe that uncertainty with probabilities too. Before seeing any data, the learner chooses a prior distribution P[θ]\mathbb P[\theta]P[θ] over the possible parameter values, saying how plausible it finds each. For example, before reading any mail you might say every frequency of “winner” in junk, from 0 to 1, is equally plausible: the uniform prior, with density 1 on [0,1][0, 1][0,1].

Given θ\thetaθ, the observations are generated as before: P[X=x∣θ]=θx(1−θ)1−x\mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta] = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}P[X=x∣θ]=θx(1−θ)1−x. Together, prior and model give a complete distribution over a single observation XXX: first draw θ\thetaθ from the prior, then XXX given θ\thetaθ. Under the uniform prior, how likely is a 1? Averaging θ\thetaθ over the prior gives 1/21/21/2. In general,

P[X=x]=∑θP[θ] P[X=x∣θ],orP[X=x]=∫P[θ] P[X=x∣θ] dθ.\mathbb P[X = x] = \sum_\theta \mathbb P[\theta]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta], \qquad \text{or} \qquad \mathbb P[X = x] = \int \mathbb P[\theta]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta]\,d\theta.P[X=x]=θ∑​P[θ]P[X=x∣θ],orP[X=x]=∫P[θ]P[X=x∣θ]dθ.
  • The sum runs over the possible parameter values, each weighted by its prior probability; when θ\thetaθ is continuous, the prior is a density and the sum becomes an integral ∫…dθ\int \dots d\theta∫…dθ, the area under the curve.
  • P[θ] P[X=x∣θ]\mathbb P[\theta]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta]P[θ]P[X=x∣θ] is the probability of “the parameter is θ\thetaθ and the observation is xxx”, by the definition of conditional probability.

In one sentence: before any data, the chance of an observation is the model’s chance averaged over the prior. Under the uniform prior, P[X=1]=∫01θ dθ=1/2\mathbb P[X = 1] = \int_0^1 \theta\,d\theta = 1/2P[X=1]=∫01​θdθ=1/2.

Here is the twist. For a frequentist, the training sequence and a fresh observation are independent: they are separate draws from one fixed distribution. For a Bayesian, they are not, because both depend on the same random θ\thetaθ. Seeing many 0s makes small θ\thetaθ more plausible, which makes the next observation more likely to be 0 too. They are independent only conditionally on θ\thetaθ: once θ\thetaθ is fixed, the draws do not influence each other. So the Bayesian’s question is: given the training sequence SSS, what is the probability of the next observation? Split by the value of θ\thetaθ:

P[X=x∣S]=∑θP[X=x∣θ,S] P[θ∣S]=∑θP[X=x∣θ] P[θ∣S].\mathbb P[X = x \mid S] = \sum_\theta \mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta, S]\,\mathbb P[\theta \mid S] = \sum_\theta \mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta]\,\mathbb P[\theta \mid S].P[X=x∣S]=θ∑​P[X=x∣θ,S]P[θ∣S]=θ∑​P[X=x∣θ]P[θ∣S].
  • P[θ∣S]\mathbb P[\theta \mid S]P[θ∣S] is the posterior distribution: how plausible each parameter is after seeing SSS.
  • The first equality is the law of total probability, applied inside the world where SSS is known: average over the possible θ\thetaθ.
  • The second drops SSS from P[X=x∣θ,S]\mathbb P[X = x \mid \theta, S]P[X=x∣θ,S], because given θ\thetaθ, the fresh XXX is independent of SSS.

In one sentence: the prediction is the model’s prediction averaged over how plausible each parameter is after the data. This is called the predictive probability.

The posterior comes from Bayes’ rule, the same identity Ines used for labels, now applied to parameters:

P[θ∣S]=P[S∣θ] P[θ]P[S]=1P[S]∏i=1mP[X=xi∣θ]  P[θ].\mathbb P[\theta \mid S] = \frac{\mathbb P[S \mid \theta]\,\mathbb P[\theta]}{\mathbb P[S]} = \frac{1}{\mathbb P[S]}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb P[X = x_i \mid \theta]\;\mathbb P[\theta].P[θ∣S]=P[S]P[S∣θ]P[θ]​=P[S]1​i=1∏m​P[X=xi​∣θ]P[θ].
  • P[S∣θ]\mathbb P[S \mid \theta]P[S∣θ] is the likelihood of θ\thetaθ, which factors into a product because the observations are independent given θ\thetaθ.
  • P[S]\mathbb P[S]P[S] is the total probability of the data, averaged over the prior; it does not depend on θ\thetaθ, so it only rescales the posterior to total 1.

In one sentence: after the data, each parameter’s plausibility is its prior plausibility times its likelihood, rescaled. For a word seen in 0 of 4 junk messages, under the uniform prior, the posterior density is proportional to (1−θ)4(1 - \theta)^4(1−θ)4: a parameter of 0.1 is now 0.94/0.54≈10.50.9^4/0.5^4 \approx 10.50.94/0.54≈10.5 times as plausible as 0.5.

Now the payoff. Put the uniform prior in, with kkk ones among mmm observations, and compute the predictive probability of a 1.

Proposition (Laplace’s rule from a uniform prior). Under the uniform prior, P[X=1∣S]=k+1m+2\mathbb P[X = 1 \mid S] = \dfrac{k + 1}{m + 2}P[X=1∣S]=m+2k+1​.

Proof. Combining the last two displays, with P[θ]=1\mathbb P[\theta] = 1P[θ]=1,

P[X=1∣S]=∫01θ⋅θk(1−θ)m−k dθ∫01θk(1−θ)m−k dθ=I(k+1,m−k)I(k,m−k),\mathbb P[X = 1 \mid S] = \frac{\int_0^1 \theta \cdot \theta^k(1-\theta)^{m-k}\,d\theta}{\int_0^1 \theta^k(1-\theta)^{m-k}\,d\theta} = \frac{I(k + 1, m - k)}{I(k, m - k)},P[X=1∣S]=∫01​θk(1−θ)m−kdθ∫01​θ⋅θk(1−θ)m−kdθ​=I(k,m−k)I(k+1,m−k)​,

where I(a,b)=∫01θa(1−θ)b dθI(a, b) = \int_0^1 \theta^a(1 - \theta)^b\,d\thetaI(a,b)=∫01​θa(1−θ)bdθ. The denominator is P[S]\mathbb P[S]P[S], the integral of prior times likelihood. The predictive probability of a 1 is the likelihood-weighted average of θ\thetaθ.

So we need I(a,b)I(a, b)I(a,b) for whole numbers a,b≥0a, b \ge 0a,b≥0. Claim: I(a,b)=a! b!(a+b+1)!I(a, b) = \dfrac{a!\,b!}{(a + b + 1)!}I(a,b)=(a+b+1)!a!b!​, where n!=1⋅2⋯nn! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots nn!=1⋅2⋯n and 0!=10! = 10!=1. For instance I(0,0)=1I(0, 0) = 1I(0,0)=1, the area of the unit square, and I(1,1)=∫01θ(1−θ) dθ=1/6I(1, 1) = \int_0^1 \theta(1-\theta)\,d\theta = 1/6I(1,1)=∫01​θ(1−θ)dθ=1/6, which the formula gives as 1⋅1/3!=1/61 \cdot 1/3! = 1/61⋅1/3!=1/6.

Integration by parts is the product rule for derivatives, integrated: ∫01u dv=[uv]01−∫01v du\int_0^1 u\,dv = [uv]_0^1 - \int_0^1 v\,du∫01​udv=[uv]01​−∫01​vdu, where [uv]01[uv]_0^1[uv]01​ is uvuvuv at 1 minus uvuvuv at 0. With u=(1−θ)bu = (1 - \theta)^bu=(1−θ)b and dv=θadθdv = \theta^a d\thetadv=θadθ, so v=θa+1/(a+1)v = \theta^{a+1}/(a + 1)v=θa+1/(a+1), gives for b≥1b \ge 1b≥1:

I(a,b)=[θa+1a+1(1−θ)b]01+ba+1∫01θa+1(1−θ)b−1 dθ=ba+1 I(a+1,b−1).I(a, b) = \left[\frac{\theta^{a+1}}{a+1}(1-\theta)^b\right]_0^1 + \frac{b}{a + 1}\int_0^1 \theta^{a+1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\,d\theta = \frac{b}{a+1}\,I(a + 1, b - 1).I(a,b)=[a+1θa+1​(1−θ)b]01​+a+1b​∫01​θa+1(1−θ)b−1dθ=a+1b​I(a+1,b−1).

The bracket is 0 at both ends (at 1 because of (1−θ)b(1-\theta)^b(1−θ)b with b≥1b \ge 1b≥1, at 0 because of θa+1\theta^{a+1}θa+1). Each step moves one power from 1−θ1 - \theta1−θ to θ\thetaθ, at the price of the factor b/(a+1)b/(a + 1)b/(a+1). For instance I(1,1)=12I(2,0)=12⋅13=16I(1, 1) = \frac12 I(2, 0) = \frac12 \cdot \frac13 = \frac16I(1,1)=21​I(2,0)=21​⋅31​=61​. Repeat bbb times: I(a,b)=ba+1⋅b−1a+2⋯1a+b I(a+b,0)I(a, b) = \frac{b}{a+1}\cdot\frac{b-1}{a+2}\cdots\frac{1}{a+b}\,I(a + b, 0)I(a,b)=a+1b​⋅a+2b−1​⋯a+b1​I(a+b,0). The numerators multiply to b!b!b!, the denominators (a+1)(a+2)⋯(a+b)(a+1)(a+2)\cdots(a+b)(a+1)(a+2)⋯(a+b) to (a+b)!/a!(a+b)!/a!(a+b)!/a!, and I(a+b,0)=∫01θa+bdθ=1/(a+b+1)I(a+b, 0) = \int_0^1 \theta^{a+b}d\theta = 1/(a + b + 1)I(a+b,0)=∫01​θa+bdθ=1/(a+b+1), so I(a,b)=a! b!(a+b)!⋅1a+b+1I(a, b) = \frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b)!}\cdot\frac{1}{a+b+1}I(a,b)=(a+b)!a!b!​⋅a+b+11​. That proves the claim.

Finally, I(k+1,m−k)I(k,m−k)=(k+1)! (m−k)!(m+2)!⋅(m+1)!k! (m−k)!=k+1m+2\dfrac{I(k+1, m-k)}{I(k, m-k)} = \dfrac{(k+1)!\,(m-k)!}{(m+2)!}\cdot\dfrac{(m+1)!}{k!\,(m-k)!} = \dfrac{k+1}{m+2}I(k,m−k)I(k+1,m−k)​=(m+2)!(k+1)!(m−k)!​⋅k!(m−k)!(m+1)!​=m+2k+1​. ■\blacksquare■

That is add-one smoothing, exactly. A word never seen in 200 junk messages gets predictive probability 1/202≈0.004951/202 \approx 0.004951/202≈0.00495, not 0. The pseudo-counts that we introduced as a regularizer are what a Bayesian with a uniform prior predicts. The prior biases the prediction toward its own average, 1/21/21/2, and the data overwhelms it as mmm grows.

import math
def I(a, b, n=100000):
    h = 1 / n
    return sum(((i + .5) * h)**a * (1 - (i + .5) * h)**b
               for i in range(n)) * h
print(round(I(1, 1), 5), round(1 / math.factorial(3), 5))
k, m = 0, 200
print(round(I(k + 1, m - k) / I(k, m - k), 5),
      round((k + 1) / (m + 2), 5))

It prints 0.16667 0.16667 and 0.00495 0.00495: a numerical integral (the midpoint rule with 100,000 slices) agrees with the formula.

Maximum a posteriori. Integrals like these rarely have closed forms. A popular shortcut keeps a single parameter: the one that maximizes the posterior,

θ^MAP∈argmax⁡θP[θ∣S]=argmax⁡θ(log⁡P[S∣θ]+log⁡P[θ]).\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}} \in \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \mathbb P[\theta \mid S] = \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \left(\log \mathbb P[S \mid \theta] + \log \mathbb P[\theta]\right).θ^MAP​∈θargmax​P[θ∣S]=θargmax​(logP[S∣θ]+logP[θ]).
  • The equality drops P[S]\mathbb P[S]P[S], which does not depend on θ\thetaθ, and takes logs, which keeps the maximizer.
  • So MAP is maximum likelihood plus a bonus log⁡P[θ]\log\mathbb P[\theta]logP[θ] from the prior: a regularizer once more.

In one sentence: the maximum a posteriori estimate is the parameter that best balances fitting the data against the prior’s preferences. With a uniform prior the bonus is constant, and MAP is plain maximum likelihood. With a strong prior, it can overrule weak data. Suppose the security team believes junk makes up more than half of all mail, and encodes this as a prior on the junk share θ\thetaθ with density 1.6 for θ≥0.5\theta \ge 0.5θ≥0.5 and 0.4 below: four times as dense on the upper half, total area 0.5⋅1.6+0.5⋅0.4=10.5 \cdot 1.6 + 0.5 \cdot 0.4 = 10.5⋅1.6+0.5⋅0.4=1. With 3 junk messages out of 10, maximum likelihood says 0.3. MAP compares 0.4⋅0.33⋅0.77≈0.000890.4 \cdot 0.3^3 \cdot 0.7^7 \approx 0.000890.4⋅0.33⋅0.77≈0.00089, the best below one half, with 1.6⋅0.510≈0.001561.6 \cdot 0.5^{10} \approx 0.001561.6⋅0.510≈0.00156, the best at or above one half, and answers 0.5. With 30 out of 100, the data wins and MAP says 0.3.

def prior(th):
    return 1.6 if th >= 0.5 else 0.4
def posterior(th, k, m):
    return prior(th) * th**k * (1 - th)**(m - k)
grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(1, 1000)]
for k, m in ((3, 10), (30, 100)):
    print(k, m, max(grid, key=lambda th: posterior(th, k, m)))

It prints 3 10 0.5 and 30 100 0.3.
