Naive Bayes

Now we can rebuild Ines’s filter on solid ground. Messages are vectors x=(x1,…,xd)x = (x_1, \dots, x_d)x=(x1​,…,xd​) of yes/no word features, labels are y∈{0,1}y \in \{0, 1\}y∈{0,1}, and the best possible hypothesis is the Bayes optimal predictor, which picks the label that is more probable given the message:

hBayes(x)=argmax⁡y∈{0,1}P[Y=y∣X=x].h_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \mathbb P[Y = y \mid X = x].hBayes​(x)=y∈{0,1}argmax​P[Y=y∣X=x].
  • XXX and YYY are the random message and label of a fresh example, and argmax⁡y∈{0,1}\operatorname*{argmax}_{y \in \{0,1\}}argmaxy∈{0,1}​ picks whichever label gives the larger probability.

In one sentence: label each message with whichever label is more probable for it, the predictor of lesson 3 recalled at the start. For “free, click”, that probability was 0.98 for junk, so it says junk.

Why not estimate P[Y=1∣X=x]\mathbb P[Y = 1 \mid X = x]P[Y=1∣X=x] directly, one number per message? Count them. With ddd yes/no words there are 2d2^d2d possible messages, so 2d2^d2d numbers to estimate. Ines’s seven words already mean 128 numbers; a dictionary of 200 words means 2200≈1.6×10602^{200} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{60}2200≈1.6×1060. Most messages would never appear in any training sequence, and the number of examples needed would grow exponentially with the number of words.

The naive Bayes assumption cuts this down with one bold simplification, the one Ines made with her independent coins: given the label, the words are independent of each other. Knowing that a junk message contains “free” tells you nothing extra about whether it contains “click”. Formally,

P[X=x∣Y=y]=∏j=1dP[Xj=xj∣Y=y].\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = y] = \prod_{j=1}^{d} \mathbb P[X_j = x_j \mid Y = y].P[X=x∣Y=y]=j=1∏d​P[Xj​=xj​∣Y=y].
  • XjX_jXj​ is the random yes/no feature for word jjj, and each factor is θj,y\theta_{j,y}θj,y​ or 1−θj,y1 - \theta_{j,y}1−θj,y​, as in Ines’s recipe; the assumption is exactly what allows the product.

In one sentence: within each kind of message, the probability of the whole message is the product of the probabilities of its words, one by one. “free, click” under junk gave 9/649/649/64.

[diagram:naive-bayes: built on the lesson page]

The assumption is called naive because it is usually false: “claim” and “prize” travel together. But it turns an impossible estimation problem into an easy one. Plug it into Bayes’ rule. The denominator of Bayes’ rule, P[X=x]\mathbb P[X = x]P[X=x], is the same for both labels, so it cannot change which label wins, and we may drop it:

hBayes(x)=argmax⁡y∈{0,1}P[Y=y] P[X=x∣Y=y]=argmax⁡y∈{0,1}P[Y=y]∏j=1dP[Xj=xj∣Y=y].h_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{y \in \{0,1\}} \mathbb P[Y = y]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = y] = \operatorname*{argmax}_{y \in \{0,1\}} \mathbb P[Y = y]\prod_{j=1}^{d}\mathbb P[X_j = x_j \mid Y = y].hBayes​(x)=y∈{0,1}argmax​P[Y=y]P[X=x∣Y=y]=y∈{0,1}argmax​P[Y=y]j=1∏d​P[Xj​=xj​∣Y=y].

The first equality is Bayes’ rule without its shared denominator; the second plugs in the naive Bayes assumption. In one sentence: pick the label whose prior share times the product of its word probabilities is larger. For “free, click” with Ines’s numbers: 0.5⋅0.1406=0.07030.5 \cdot 0.1406 = 0.07030.5⋅0.1406=0.0703 against 0.00150.00150.0015, junk.

Now count parameters: one prior share P[Y=1]\mathbb P[Y = 1]P[Y=1], plus θj,y\theta_{j,y}θj,y​ for ddd words and 2 labels. That is 2d+12d + 12d+1, instead of 2d2^d2d. For 200 words, 401 numbers. The generative assumption has done what an inductive bias always does: it bought a small number of parameters with a strong belief about the world.

When the parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (the counted fractions, as Ines did), the result is the classical naive Bayes classifier. You now know that this is exactly the version that crashes, and that the right estimator for each θj,y\theta_{j,y}θj,y​ is θ^α\hat\theta_\alphaθ^α​ with α>0\alpha > 0α>0. In what follows the naive Bayes filter means naive Bayes with add-α\alphaα estimates.

Rerun Ines’s two bug-report messages with add-one estimates, which we can now do with confidence:

import math
W = ["free", "prize", "click", "invoice",
     "meeting", "lunch", "winner"]
junk = [{"free", "prize", "click"}, {"free", "click"},
        {"prize", "click"}, {"free", "prize"}]
keep = [{"meeting", "lunch"}, {"invoice", "meeting"},
        {"lunch", "click"}, {"free", "lunch", "meeting"}]
def freq(msgs, a):
    m = len(msgs)
    return {w: (sum(w in x for x in msgs) + a) / (m + 2 * a)
            for w in W}
def P(x, th):
    return math.prod(th[w] if w in x else 1 - th[w] for w in W)
th1, th0 = freq(junk, 1), freq(keep, 1)
for x in ({"free", "click", "meeting"}, {"winner", "click"}):
    p1, p0 = 0.5 * P(x, th1), 0.5 * P(x, th0)
    print(sorted(x), round(p1 / (p1 + p0), 3))

It prints ['click', 'free', 'meeting'] 0.556 and ['click', 'winner'] 0.758. The junk-looking message with “meeting” in it is now junk with probability 0.556: “meeting” is real evidence for keep and “free, click” real evidence for junk, and four examples per pile can only weigh them so finely. That is a hedge, not a certainty. “winner, click” no longer crashes: “winner” is equally unknown to both piles, so it cancels out, and “click” tips the balance toward junk.

A guarantee for the whole filter. The pseudo-count theorem speaks about one parameter. The filter has 2d2d2d word parameters, and we want all of them to behave at once. Lesson 2’s union bound does it: the probability that at least one of several bad events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities. Suppose your users label mmm messages of each kind, and the share of junk P[Y=1]\mathbb P[Y = 1]P[Y=1] is known from traffic logs, so only the 2d2d2d word frequencies are estimated. Apply part (a) of the theorem to each of them with confidence δ/(2d)\delta/(2d)δ/(2d) instead of δ\deltaδ. Each fails with probability at most δ/(2d)\delta/(2d)δ/(2d), so all 2d2d2d hold together with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ:

PS[∀j∈[d], ∀y∈{0,1}: ∣θ^j,y−θj,y⋆∣≤log⁡(4d/δ)2m+αm+2α]≥1−δ.\mathbb P_S\left[\forall j \in [d],\ \forall y \in \{0,1\}:\ |\hat\theta_{j,y} - \theta^\star_{j,y}| \le \sqrt{\frac{\log(4d/\delta)}{2m}} + \frac{\alpha}{m + 2\alpha}\right] \ge 1 - \delta.PS​[∀j∈[d], ∀y∈{0,1}: ∣θ^j,y​−θj,y⋆​∣≤2mlog(4d/δ)​​+m+2αα​]≥1−δ.
  • ∀\forall∀ reads “for every”, and [d][d][d] is the set of word positions {1,…,d}\{1, \dots, d\}{1,…,d}, as [m][m][m] was in lesson 1.
  • θj,y⋆\theta^\star_{j,y}θj,y⋆​ is the true frequency of word jjj in messages of kind yyy, and θ^j,y\hat\theta_{j,y}θ^j,y​ its add-α\alphaα estimate from the mmm messages of that kind.
  • log⁡(4d/δ)\log(4d/\delta)log(4d/δ) is log⁡(2/δ′)\log(2/\delta')log(2/δ′) with δ′=δ/(2d)\delta' = \delta/(2d)δ′=δ/(2d): the price of the union bound is a logarithm of the number of parameters.

In one sentence: with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, every word frequency in both piles is estimated within the same distance of the truth. Part (b), meanwhile, needs no union bound, because it is a statement about each word’s expected excess risk: every word, seen or unseen, costs at most (m/4+α2)/(α(m+α))(m/4 + \alpha^2)/(\alpha(m + \alpha))(m/4+α2)/(α(m+α)) nats of expected excess log loss. With d=200d = 200d=200, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, m=600m = 600m=600 and α=1\alpha = 1α=1: every frequency within 0.09150.09150.0915, and every word’s expected excess at most 0.25120.25120.2512 nats.

Naive Bayes as code

Training only counts. Prediction adds logarithms instead of multiplying probabilities, so that 200 small factors do not underflow to 0, and compares the two sums.

NaiveBayesTrain(S, d, α):
  for y in {0, 1}:
    m_y ← number of examples in S with label y
    for j = 1..d:
      k ← number of examples with label y and x_j = 1
      θ[j, y] ← (k + α) / (m_y + 2α)
  return θ

NaiveBayesPredict(θ, π, x):
  for y in {0, 1}:
    s[y] ← log(π_y)
    for j = 1..d:
      s[y] ← s[y] + log(θ[j, y]) if x_j = 1
                    else log(1 − θ[j, y])
  return 1 if s[1] > s[0] else 0

Here π1=P[Y=1]\pi_1 = \mathbb P[Y = 1]π1​=P[Y=1] and π0=1−π1\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1π0​=1−π1​ are the prior shares, known or estimated by counting. The probability of junk, if you want it rather than the label, is 1/(1+es[0]−s[1])1/(1 + e^{s[0] - s[1]})1/(1+es[0]−s[1]), which is Bayes’ rule divided through by its numerator.

Training reads every feature of every example once: O(md)O(md)O(md) time, and O(d)O(d)O(d) space for the 2d2d2d counts. Prediction is O(d)O(d)O(d) time per message. A message usually contains only a few dictionary words, and that can be exploited: precompute By=∑jlog⁡(1−θj,y)B_y = \sum_j \log(1 - \theta_{j,y})By​=∑j​log(1−θj,y​) once, and then for each word present add log⁡θj,y−log⁡(1−θj,y)\log\theta_{j,y} - \log(1 - \theta_{j,y})logθj,y​−log(1−θj,y​). Prediction then costs time proportional to the number of words in the message. Notice also what α>0\alpha > 0α>0 does for the code: every θ\thetaθ is strictly between 0 and 1, so every log⁡\loglog is finite, and the crash is impossible by construction rather than by luck.

Compare this with every learner since lesson 9. There is no optimization at all: no gradient, no iterations, no convergence to worry about. That is the computational argument for generative models from the start of the lesson, in its purest form.

Build it yourself. Using only the Python standard library:

import math

W = ["free", "prize", "click", "invoice",
     "meeting", "lunch", "winner"]
S = [({"free", "prize", "click"}, 1), ({"free", "click"}, 1),
     ({"prize", "click"}, 1), ({"free", "prize"}, 1),
     ({"meeting", "lunch"}, 0), ({"invoice", "meeting"}, 0),
     ({"lunch", "click"}, 0), ({"free", "lunch", "meeting"}, 0)]

def train(S, words, alpha): ...
def junk_probability(theta, prior, x, words): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    theta = train(S, W, 1)
    assert theta[("winner", 1)] == 1 / 6
    assert theta[("free", 0)] == 2 / 6
    p = junk_probability(theta, 0.5, {"winner", "click"}, W)
    assert round(p, 3) == 0.758
    p = junk_probability(theta, 0.5, {"lunch", "meeting"}, W)
    assert round(p, 3) == 0.008
    theta0 = train(S, W, 0)
    p = junk_probability(theta0, 0.5, {"free", "click"}, W)
    assert round(p, 3) == 0.98
  1. Implement train, returning a dictionary keyed by (word, label), and junk_probability, working in logarithms and returning P[Y=1∣x]\mathbb P[Y = 1 \mid x]P[Y=1∣x].
  2. With alpha = 0, decide what junk_probability should do on “winner, click”. Raise a clear exception? Return None? Write down why each choice is worse than smoothing.
  3. Build the 200-word world of the lab: word jjj (from 0) with rank r=j+1r = j + 1r=j+1 has frequency 0.6 r−0.80.6\,r^{-0.8}0.6r−0.8 in junk and 0.15 r−0.80.15\,r^{-0.8}0.15r−0.8 in keep when jjj is even, the other way round when jjj is odd. Draw training sequences and fresh messages, and measure how often maximum likelihood crashes for m=10,30,100,300,1000m = 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000m=10,30,100,300,1000 messages per kind.
  4. Implement the sparse prediction trick and check it returns the same probabilities.

Fix the bug

Ines is back, and she has the 200-word dictionary from the lab, with its long tail of rare words. Users will label up to 600 messages of each kind; the traffic logs say half of all mail is junk, so the prior share is known. Your manager will ship the filter only with a certificate from this lesson’s theorems, holding for every possible set of true word frequencies, not just for the frequencies in this week’s mail:

  1. Accurate: with probability at least 95%, every one of the 400 word frequencies is estimated within 0.1 of the truth.
  2. Safe on unseen words: every word, including words never seen in training, has expected excess log loss at most 0.4 nats.

You choose two things: the number mmm of labelled messages of each kind, and the estimator, given by its pseudo-count α\alphaα. Here are both certificates as code, so you can work out the settings before you try them:

import math
d, delta = 200, 0.05
def accuracy(m, a):
    return math.sqrt(math.log(4 * d / delta) / (2 * m)) \
        + a / (m + 2 * a)
def excess(m, a):
    return math.inf if a == 0 else (m / 4 + a * a) / (a * (m + a))
for m, a in ((600, 0), (600, 0.5), (600, 1), (400, 1), (600, 20)):
    print(m, a, round(accuracy(m, a), 4), round(excess(m, a), 4))

It prints:

600 0 0.0898 inf
600 0.5 0.0906 0.5004
600 1 0.0915 0.2512
400 1 0.1125 0.2519
600 20 0.1211 0.0444

Read the rows before you open the lab. Maximum likelihood is accurate and has no certificate at all on unseen words. Half a pseudo-count is not enough. Too few labels break the accuracy certificate, and so do too many pseudo-counts.

In the lab, each round draws a fresh set of true frequencies and a fresh training sequence. A setting that happens to classify this round’s test messages well does not pass; only a setting whose certificates meet both targets does.

Another assumption: Gaussian clouds

Naive Bayes is one generative assumption. Here is a second, for measured features, and it leads somewhere you have been before.

Suppose the mail room scores every message on two measured features: the capitals score x1x_1x1​ (how shouty the subject is) and the link score x2x_2x2​ (how many links, scaled). Plot keep messages and they form an elliptical cloud around (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1); plot junk and they form a cloud of the same shape around (3,2)(3, 2)(3,2). In both clouds the two scores tend to rise together: a shouty message tends to have more links.

To describe a cloud like this we need the Gaussian in ddd dimensions. Its centre is a vector μ∈Rd\mu \in \mathbb R^dμ∈Rd. Its shape is a covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ, a d×dd \times dd×d table: on the diagonal, the variance of each score (its spread); off the diagonal, the covariance of each pair of scores, positive when they tend to rise together. For our clouds,

Σ=(10.50.51):\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}:Σ=(10.5​0.51​):

each score has variance 1, and the two scores have covariance 0.5. The density of the Gaussian with centre μ\muμ and covariance Σ\SigmaΣ is

P[X=x]=1(2π)d/2 ∣Σ∣1/2exp⁡(−12(x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ)).\mathbb P[X = x] = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac12 (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu)\right).P[X=x]=(2π)d/2∣Σ∣1/21​exp(−21​(x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ)).
  • x−μx - \mux−μ is the offset of the message from the centre, a column vector; (x−μ)⊤(x - \mu)^\top(x−μ)⊤ is the same offset written as a row (the ⊤\top⊤ means transpose).
  • Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1 is the inverse matrix of Σ\SigmaΣ, the matrix with Σ−1Σ=I\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma = IΣ−1Σ=I, the identity. The product (x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ)(x - \mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu)(x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ) is a single number: a squared distance in which directions where the cloud is wide count less, and directions where it is narrow count more. With Σ=I\Sigma = IΣ=I it is the ordinary squared distance ∥x−μ∥2\|x - \mu\|^2∥x−μ∥2.
  • ∣Σ∣|\Sigma|∣Σ∣ is the determinant of Σ\SigmaΣ, a measure of the cloud’s volume; with the factor (2π)d/2(2\pi)^{d/2}(2π)d/2 it makes the total volume under the density equal to 1.

In one sentence: a Gaussian cloud is densest at its centre and thins out with the stretched squared distance from it. For d=1d = 1d=1 this is the bell from before. At the centre of our clouds, the density is 1/(2π0.75)≈0.1841/(2\pi\sqrt{0.75}) \approx 0.1841/(2π0.75​)≈0.184.

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) makes three generative assumptions: the two labels are equally likely, P[Y=1]=P[Y=0]=1/2\mathbb P[Y = 1] = \mathbb P[Y = 0] = 1/2P[Y=1]=P[Y=0]=1/2; given the label yyy, the message is Gaussian with centre μy\mu_yμy​; and the covariance Σ\SigmaΣ is the same for both labels. Under these assumptions, what does the Bayes optimal predictor look like?

It predicts junk when P[Y=1] P[X=x∣Y=1]>P[Y=0] P[X=x∣Y=0]\mathbb P[Y = 1]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = 1] > \mathbb P[Y = 0]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = 0]P[Y=1]P[X=x∣Y=1]>P[Y=0]P[X=x∣Y=0], that is, when the ratio of the two sides is above 1, that is, when its logarithm is above 0. That logarithm is the log-likelihood ratio:

log⁡(P[Y=1] P[X=x∣Y=1]P[Y=0] P[X=x∣Y=0])=12(x−μ0)⊤Σ−1(x−μ0)−12(x−μ1)⊤Σ−1(x−μ1).\log\left(\frac{\mathbb P[Y = 1]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = 1]}{\mathbb P[Y = 0]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = 0]}\right) = \frac12(x - \mu_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu_0) - \frac12(x - \mu_1)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu_1).log(P[Y=0]P[X=x∣Y=0]P[Y=1]P[X=x∣Y=1]​)=21​(x−μ0​)⊤Σ−1(x−μ0​)−21​(x−μ1​)⊤Σ−1(x−μ1​).
  • On the left, the prior shares are equal and cancel, and so do the normalizing constants (2π)d/2∣Σ∣1/2(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}(2π)d/2∣Σ∣1/2, because Σ\SigmaΣ is shared.
  • What is left is the log of a ratio of two exponentials, which is the difference of their exponents.

In one sentence: the evidence for junk is how much closer the message is to the junk centre than to the keep centre, in stretched distance. For the message x=(3,2)x = (3, 2)x=(3,2), sitting on the junk centre, its stretched squared distance to the keep centre is (2,1)Σ−1(2,1)⊤=4(2, 1)\Sigma^{-1}(2, 1)^\top = 4(2,1)Σ−1(2,1)⊤=4 and to the junk centre 0, so the ratio’s log is 12⋅4=2\frac12 \cdot 4 = 221​⋅4=2: junk is e2≈7.4e^2 \approx 7.4e2≈7.4 times as likely.

Now expand both stretched distances. Each is x⊤Σ−1x−2μy⊤Σ−1x+μy⊤Σ−1μyx^\top\Sigma^{-1}x - 2\mu_y^\top\Sigma^{-1}x + \mu_y^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_yx⊤Σ−1x−2μy⊤​Σ−1x+μy⊤​Σ−1μy​, where the middle term combines x⊤Σ−1μyx^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_yx⊤Σ−1μy​ and μy⊤Σ−1x\mu_y^\top\Sigma^{-1}xμy⊤​Σ−1x, which are equal because Σ\SigmaΣ, and hence Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1, is symmetric. The x⊤Σ−1xx^\top\Sigma^{-1}xx⊤Σ−1x terms cancel between the two halves, and the log-likelihood ratio is ⟨w,x⟩+b\langle w, x\rangle + b⟨w,x⟩+b with

w=Σ−1(μ1−μ0),b=12(μ0⊤Σ−1μ0−μ1⊤Σ−1μ1).w = \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0), \qquad b = \frac12\left(\mu_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_0 - \mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1\right).w=Σ−1(μ1​−μ0​),b=21​(μ0⊤​Σ−1μ0​−μ1⊤​Σ−1μ1​).
  • ⟨w,x⟩=∑jwjxj\langle w, x\rangle = \sum_j w_j x_j⟨w,x⟩=∑j​wj​xj​ is the inner product of lesson 9: a weighted sum of the scores.
  • www points from the keep centre to the junk centre, then is reshaped by Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1 to account for the clouds’ correlations.
  • bbb is a constant: it puts the boundary halfway between the clouds, in stretched distance.

In one sentence: under the LDA assumptions, the Bayes optimal predictor is a halfspace: junk exactly when a weighted sum of the scores exceeds a threshold. For our clouds, Σ−1=10.75(1−0.5−0.51)\Sigma^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.75}\begin{pmatrix}1 & -0.5\\ -0.5 & 1\end{pmatrix}Σ−1=0.751​(1−0.5​−0.51​), μ1−μ0=(2,1)\mu_1 - \mu_0 = (2, 1)μ1​−μ0​=(2,1), so w=(2,0)w = (2, 0)w=(2,0), and b=12(43−283)=−4b = \frac12(\frac43 - \frac{28}{3}) = -4b=21​(34​−328​)=−4. Junk exactly when 2x1−4>02x_1 - 4 > 02x1​−4>0, that is, when the capitals score exceeds 2.

[diagram:lda: built on the lesson page]

Look at that www: the link score gets weight 0, even though junk has more links on average. The reason is the correlation. Given the capitals score, the extra links of junk are just what the shared cloud shape predicts from its shoutiness, so they carry no further evidence. A rule that weighs each score by its own difference in means would get this wrong.

import math
mu0, mu1 = (1, 1), (3, 2)
inv = [[1 / .75, -.5 / .75], [-.5 / .75, 1 / .75]]
def quad(v):
    return sum(v[i] * inv[i][j] * v[j]
               for i in range(2) for j in range(2))
def log_ratio(x):
    d0 = [x[i] - mu0[i] for i in range(2)]
    d1 = [x[i] - mu1[i] for i in range(2)]
    return 0.5 * quad(d0) - 0.5 * quad(d1)
dm = [mu1[i] - mu0[i] for i in range(2)]
w = [sum(inv[i][j] * dm[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)]
b = 0.5 * (quad(mu0) - quad(mu1))
pts = [(a / 4, c / 4)
       for a in range(-8, 24) for c in range(-8, 24)]
print([round(v, 6) for v in w], round(b, 6),
      round(log_ratio(mu1), 3))
print(max(abs(log_ratio(x) - (w[0] * x[0] + w[1] * x[1] + b))
          for x in pts) < 1e-9)

It prints [2.0, 0.0] -4.0 2.0 and True: on 1,024 grid points, the difference of stretched distances and the linear rule agree.

So a generative assumption has rederived the hypothesis class of lesson 9. The difference is in how the halfspace is chosen. LDA does not search for a good www; it estimates the centres and the covariance, and computes www and bbb from them. The usual estimates are the maximum likelihood ones: each centre is the average of its class, and the shared covariance is the average, over all mmm examples, of the outer product of each example’s offset v=xi−μyiv = x_i - \mu_{y_i}v=xi​−μyi​​ from its own class centre. The outer product vv⊤vv^\topvv⊤ is the d×dd \times dd×d matrix with entry vjvkv_j v_kvj​vk​ in row jjj, column kkk, as in lesson 23; for the offset (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) it is (1000)\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}(10​00​).

LDATrain(S):
  for y in {0, 1}:
    μ[y] ← average of the x_i with y_i = y
  Σ ← (1/m) · sum over i of (x_i − μ[y_i])(x_i − μ[y_i])ᵀ
  w ← solve Σ w = μ[1] − μ[0]
  b ← ½ (μ[0]ᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ[0] − μ[1]ᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ[1])
  return (w, b)

LDAPredict(w, b, x):
  return 1 if ⟨w, x⟩ + b > 0 else 0

Cost. The centres take O(md)O(md)O(md) time, the covariance O(md2)O(md^2)O(md2) (one d×dd \times dd×d outer product per example), and solving the linear system O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3) by Gaussian elimination; space is O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) for Σ\SigmaΣ. Prediction is O(d)O(d)O(d), like any halfspace. For bbb, note that μy⊤Σ−1μy\mu_y^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_yμy⊤​Σ−1μy​ can reuse the solved system: b=−12⟨w,μ1+μ0⟩b = -\tfrac12\langle w, \mu_1 + \mu_0\rangleb=−21​⟨w,μ1​+μ0​⟩, because μ0⊤Σ−1μ0−μ1⊤Σ−1μ1=−(μ1−μ0)⊤Σ−1(μ1+μ0)\mu_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_0 - \mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1 = -(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 + \mu_0)μ0⊤​Σ−1μ0​−μ1⊤​Σ−1μ1​=−(μ1​−μ0​)⊤Σ−1(μ1​+μ0​) by symmetry of Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1.

Build it yourself. In the standard library, for d=2d = 2d=2:

S = [((2, 2), 0), ((0, 0), 0), ((2, 1), 0), ((0, 1), 0),
     ((4, 3), 1), ((2, 1), 1), ((4, 2), 1), ((2, 2), 1)]

def lda_train(S): ...
def lda_predict(w, b, x): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    w, b = lda_train(S)
    assert [round(v, 6) for v in w] == [2.0, 0.0]
    assert round(b, 6) == -4.0
    assert lda_predict(w, b, (3, 2)) == 1
    assert lda_predict(w, b, (1, 1)) == 0
  1. Implement lda_train (class means, pooled covariance, a 2 by 2 inverse) and lda_predict.
  2. Draw 2,000 messages from the two clouds of this section (use random.gauss on independent coordinates and mix them to get covariance 0.5) and check that the estimated www approaches (2,0)(2, 0)(2,0) as mmm grows.
  3. Break the shared-covariance assumption: give junk a wider cloud. Compare LDA’s error with the Bayes optimal predictor’s, computed from the true densities.

Hidden causes: latent variables

So far every example came with its label. Now look at the unlabelled archive: a million messages nobody ever clicked on. The product team suspects there are two kinds of message in it, newsletters and personal notes, with different length scores, but no message says which kind it is. The kind is a latent variable: part of the story of how the message was produced, but never observed.

A model with a latent variable tells the production story in two steps. First, choose the kind: kind yyy with probability cyc_ycy​, for yyy in {1,…,k}\{1, \dots, k\}{1,…,k}. Second, write a message of that kind: draw xxx from a Gaussian with centre μy\mu_yμy​ and covariance Σy\Sigma_yΣy​. With two kinds, a newsletter share of c2=0.3c_2 = 0.3c2​=0.3, and centres 1 and 4 on the length score, you get a two-humped density. The probability (density) of a message adds over the kinds that could have produced it:

P[X=x]=∑y=1kP[Y=y] P[X=x∣Y=y]=∑y=1kcy 1(2π)d/2∣Σy∣1/2exp⁡(−12(x−μy)⊤Σy−1(x−μy)).\mathbb P[X = x] = \sum_{y=1}^{k}\mathbb P[Y = y]\,\mathbb P[X = x \mid Y = y] = \sum_{y=1}^{k} c_y\,\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma_y|^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac12(x - \mu_y)^\top\Sigma_y^{-1}(x - \mu_y)\right).P[X=x]=y=1∑k​P[Y=y]P[X=x∣Y=y]=y=1∑k​cy​(2π)d/2∣Σy​∣1/21​exp(−21​(x−μy​)⊤Σy−1​(x−μy​)).
  • YYY is the latent kind and cy=P[Y=y]c_y = \mathbb P[Y = y]cy​=P[Y=y] its share; the cyc_ycy​ are nonnegative and add up to 1.
  • The first equality is the law of total probability: a message arises by some kind, so add the chances over the kinds. Each term is then a share times a Gaussian cloud of the previous section.

In one sentence: a mixture of Gaussians is a weighted sum of bells, one per hidden kind. At x=1x = 1x=1, with c=(0.7,0.3)c = (0.7, 0.3)c=(0.7,0.3), centres 1 and 4 and width 1: 0.7⋅0.399+0.3⋅0.0044≈0.2810.7 \cdot 0.399 + 0.3 \cdot 0.0044 \approx 0.2810.7⋅0.399+0.3⋅0.0044≈0.281.

Let θ\thetaθ collect all the parameters (the shares, centres and covariances). For an i.i.d. sample S=(x1,…,xm)S = (x_1, \dots, x_m)S=(x1​,…,xm​), the log-likelihood is

L(θ)=∑i=1mlog⁡Pθ[X=xi]=∑i=1mlog⁡(∑y=1kPθ[X=xi,Y=y]).L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\log \mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i] = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\left(\sum_{y=1}^{k}\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]\right).L(θ)=i=1∑m​logPθ​[X=xi​]=i=1∑m​log(y=1∑k​Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y]).
  • Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y] is the joint probability that the kind is yyy and the message is xix_ixi​: cyc_ycy​ times the yyy-th bell at xix_ixi​.
  • The outer sum adds one log per example; the inner sum, inside the log, adds over the kinds.

In one sentence: the log-likelihood adds, over messages, the log of the total chance of each message over all the kinds that might have produced it. For the single message x=1x = 1x=1 in the mixture above, L=log⁡0.281≈−1.27L = \log 0.281 \approx -1.27L=log0.281≈−1.27. Maximum likelihood wants the θ\thetaθ that maximizes it.

The sum inside the logarithm is the trouble. Without it, the log of each joint probability would split into simple pieces, and maximizing would be as easy as for LDA: if we knew each message’s kind, we would just average each kind’s messages. With it, there is no closed form, and in many cases the optimization is computationally hard. The Expectation-Maximization algorithm, EM, due to Dempster, Laird and Rubin, is an iterative way to search for a maximum. It may stop at a local maximum rather than the global one, but it often works well in practice.

EM’s idea is a chicken-and-egg loop. If we knew the kinds, finding θ\thetaθ would be easy. If we knew θ\thetaθ, we could compute, for each message, how probable each kind is. So alternate. To say it precisely, replace “the kind of message iii” by a soft assignment: a probability vector Qi,1,…,Qi,kQ_{i,1}, \dots, Q_{i,k}Qi,1​,…,Qi,k​ over the kinds for each message, collected in an m×km \times km×k matrix QQQ whose rows add up to 1. Then define the expected complete log-likelihood:

F(Q,θ)=∑i=1m∑y=1kQi,ylog⁡(Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]).F(Q, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{y=1}^{k} Q_{i,y}\log\left(\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]\right).F(Q,θ)=i=1∑m​y=1∑k​Qi,y​log(Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y]).
  • For each message iii and kind yyy, log⁡Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]\log\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]logPθ​[X=xi​,Y=y] is what the log-likelihood would be if we knew that message iii has kind yyy.
  • Qi,yQ_{i,y}Qi,y​ weights it by how much we currently believe that. So FFF is the expected log-likelihood of a labelled data set whose labels are drawn from the rows of QQQ.
  • The sum over kinds is now outside the log.

In one sentence: FFF is the log-likelihood we would have if the hidden kinds were known, averaged over our current beliefs about them. With one message x=1x = 1x=1, the belief Q=(0.9,0.1)Q = (0.9, 0.1)Q=(0.9,0.1), and the mixture above: 0.9log⁡(0.7⋅0.399)+0.1log⁡(0.3⋅0.0044)≈−1.810.9\log(0.7 \cdot 0.399) + 0.1\log(0.3 \cdot 0.0044) \approx -1.810.9log(0.7⋅0.399)+0.1log(0.3⋅0.0044)≈−1.81.

We assume, as is true for Gaussian mixtures, that for any fixed QQQ with rows adding to 1, maximizing F(Q,θ)F(Q, \theta)F(Q,θ) over θ\thetaθ is tractable. EM builds a sequence (Q(1),θ(1)),(Q(2),θ(2)),…(Q^{(1)}, \theta^{(1)}), (Q^{(2)}, \theta^{(2)}), \dots(Q(1),θ(1)),(Q(2),θ(2)),…; the superscript (t)(t)(t) is the iteration number. Each iteration does two steps:

E step:Qi,y(t+1)=Pθ(t)[Y=y∣X=xi],M step:θ(t+1)∈argmax⁡θF(Q(t+1),θ).\text{E step:}\quad Q^{(t+1)}_{i,y} = \mathbb P_{\theta^{(t)}}[Y = y \mid X = x_i], \qquad \text{M step:}\quad \theta^{(t+1)} \in \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta F(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta).E step:Qi,y(t+1)​=Pθ(t)​[Y=y∣X=xi​],M step:θ(t+1)∈θargmax​F(Q(t+1),θ).
  • The E step (expectation) sets each soft assignment to the probability of each kind given the message, under the current parameters, by Bayes’ rule. It defines the new expected log-likelihood F(Q(t+1),⋅)F(Q^{(t+1)}, \cdot)F(Q(t+1),⋅).
  • The M step (maximization) finds the parameters that maximize that expected log-likelihood, which is tractable by assumption.

In one sentence: guess the hidden kinds from the parameters, then refit the parameters to the guessed kinds, and repeat. The starting values are usually random, and the loop stops when the log-likelihood stops improving noticeably.

Why EM never goes downhill

An iterative algorithm with no guarantee is a hope. EM comes with one: the log-likelihood never decreases. The proof is short once we see EM as climbing a different function, one coordinate at a time. The plan: build a function GGG of the beliefs and the parameters that is never above the log-likelihood, touches it whenever the beliefs are the E step’s, and goes up at every step. Then the log-likelihood, which GGG touches after every E step, must go up too.

Define, with the convention 0log⁡0=00 \log 0 = 00log0=0,

G(Q,θ)=F(Q,θ)−∑i=1m∑y=1kQi,ylog⁡Qi,y=∑i=1m∑y=1kQi,ylog⁡Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]Qi,y.G(Q, \theta) = F(Q, \theta) - \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{y=1}^{k} Q_{i,y}\log Q_{i,y} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{y=1}^{k} Q_{i,y}\log\frac{\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]}{Q_{i,y}}.G(Q,θ)=F(Q,θ)−i=1∑m​y=1∑k​Qi,y​logQi,y​=i=1∑m​y=1∑k​Qi,y​logQi,y​Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y]​.
  • The subtracted double sum is minus the sum of the entropies of the rows of QQQ: a bonus for soft assignments that are uncertain.
  • The second form combines the two logs into one; terms with Qi,y=0Q_{i,y} = 0Qi,y​=0 are left out.

In one sentence: GGG is the expected complete log-likelihood plus the entropy of the beliefs. Let Q\mathcal QQ be the set of m×km \times km×k matrices with entries in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] whose rows add up to 1, the allowed soft assignments.

Lemma (EM is alternate maximization). The two EM steps are Q(t+1)∈argmax⁡Q∈QG(Q,θ(t))Q^{(t+1)} \in \operatorname*{argmax}_{Q \in \mathcal Q} G(Q, \theta^{(t)})Q(t+1)∈argmaxQ∈Q​G(Q,θ(t)) and θ(t+1)∈argmax⁡θG(Q(t+1),θ)\theta^{(t+1)} \in \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta G(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta)θ(t+1)∈argmaxθ​G(Q(t+1),θ). Moreover, G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t))G(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t)}) = L(\theta^{(t)})G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t)).

Proof. The M step first. The entropy term of GGG does not involve θ\thetaθ, so for fixed Q(t+1)Q^{(t+1)}Q(t+1), maximizing GGG over θ\thetaθ is the same as maximizing FFF. That is the M step.

The E step. Fix any θ\thetaθ and any Q∈QQ \in \mathcal QQ∈Q. We show G(Q,θ)≤L(θ)G(Q, \theta) \le L(\theta)G(Q,θ)≤L(θ), and then that the E step’s choice reaches it.

For the inequality, fix a message iii and write ay=Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]a_y = \mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]ay​=Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y] and A=∑yay=Pθ[X=xi]A = \sum_y a_y = \mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i]A=∑y​ay​=Pθ​[X=xi​]. Using log⁡t≤t−1\log t \le t - 1logt≤t−1 from the relative-entropy proof, with t=ay/(Qi,yA)t = a_y/(Q_{i,y}A)t=ay​/(Qi,y​A), on the kinds with Qi,y>0Q_{i,y} > 0Qi,y​>0:

∑y:Qi,y>0Qi,ylog⁡ayQi,yA≤∑y:Qi,y>0Qi,y(ayQi,yA−1)=∑y:Qi,y>0ayA−1≤0.\sum_{y : Q_{i,y} > 0} Q_{i,y}\log\frac{a_y}{Q_{i,y}A} \le \sum_{y : Q_{i,y} > 0} Q_{i,y}\left(\frac{a_y}{Q_{i,y}A} - 1\right) = \sum_{y : Q_{i,y} > 0}\frac{a_y}{A} - 1 \le 0.y:Qi,y​>0∑​Qi,y​logQi,y​Aay​​≤y:Qi,y​>0∑​Qi,y​(Qi,y​Aay​​−1)=y:Qi,y​>0∑​Aay​​−1≤0.
  • The left side is message iii’s part of GGG, minus log⁡A\log AlogA (because the Qi,yQ_{i,y}Qi,y​ add up to 1, ∑yQi,ylog⁡A=log⁡A\sum_y Q_{i,y}\log A = \log A∑y​Qi,y​logA=logA).
  • The middle step multiplies out: each Qi,yQ_{i,y}Qi,y​ cancels, and the Qi,yQ_{i,y}Qi,y​ themselves add up to 1.
  • The last step holds because the aya_yay​ over some kinds add up to at most AAA.

In one sentence: any soft assignment explains message iii at most as well as the true total chance of message iii. This is Jensen’s inequality for the logarithm, in the special form we need. Adding over iii: G(Q,θ)≤∑ilog⁡Pθ[X=xi]=L(θ)G(Q, \theta) \le \sum_i \log\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i] = L(\theta)G(Q,θ)≤∑i​logPθ​[X=xi​]=L(θ).

For the equality, put Qi,y=Pθ[Y=y∣X=xi]Q_{i,y} = \mathbb P_\theta[Y = y \mid X = x_i]Qi,y​=Pθ​[Y=y∣X=xi​]. By the definition of conditional probability, Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]=Pθ[Y=y∣X=xi] Pθ[X=xi]\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y] = \mathbb P_\theta[Y = y \mid X = x_i]\,\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i]Pθ​[X=xi​,Y=y]=Pθ​[Y=y∣X=xi​]Pθ​[X=xi​], so the ratio inside the log of GGG is Pθ[X=xi]\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i]Pθ​[X=xi​] for every yyy, and

G(Q,θ)=∑i=1mlog⁡Pθ[X=xi]∑y=1kPθ[Y=y∣X=xi]=∑i=1mlog⁡Pθ[X=xi]=L(θ),G(Q, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i]\sum_{y=1}^{k}\mathbb P_\theta[Y = y \mid X = x_i] = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i] = L(\theta),G(Q,θ)=i=1∑m​logPθ​[X=xi​]y=1∑k​Pθ​[Y=y∣X=xi​]=i=1∑m​logPθ​[X=xi​]=L(θ),

since conditional probabilities over all kinds add up to 1. With the E step’s beliefs, GGG equals the log-likelihood exactly. (For a Gaussian mixture every joint probability is positive, so no terms are dropped.) So the E step’s QQQ attains the upper bound L(θ)L(\theta)L(θ): it maximizes G(⋅,θ)G(\cdot, \theta)G(⋅,θ) over Q\mathcal QQ, and G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t))G(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t)}) = L(\theta^{(t)})G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t)). ■\blacksquare■

Here is the lemma on the one-message example from the previous section, x=1x = 1x=1 with shares (0.7,0.3)(0.7, 0.3)(0.7,0.3) and centres 1 and 4: the mixture density, FFF and GGG for the belief (0.9,0.1)(0.9, 0.1)(0.9,0.1), and GGG for the E step’s belief, against the log-likelihood.

import math
c, mu, x = (0.7, 0.3), (1.0, 4.0), 1.0
def bell(x, m):
    return math.exp(-(x - m)**2 / 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
a = [c[y] * bell(x, mu[y]) for y in (0, 1)]
L = math.log(sum(a))
def F(Q):
    return sum(Q[y] * math.log(a[y]) for y in (0, 1))
def G(Q):
    return F(Q) - sum(q * math.log(q) for q in Q if q > 0)
post = [v / sum(a) for v in a]
print(round(sum(a), 3), round(F((0.9, 0.1)), 2))
print(round(G((0.9, 0.1)), 3), round(G(post), 3), round(L, 3))

It prints 0.281 -1.81, then -1.485 -1.271 -1.271: the guessed belief gives a GGG below the log-likelihood, and the E step’s belief, (0.995,0.005)(0.995, 0.005)(0.995,0.005), meets it exactly.

Theorem (EM never decreases the likelihood). For every ttt, L(θ(t+1))≥L(θ(t))L(\theta^{(t+1)}) \ge L(\theta^{(t)})L(θ(t+1))≥L(θ(t)).

Proof. Three links, each from the lemma:

L(θ(t+1))=G(Q(t+2),θ(t+1))≥G(Q(t+1),θ(t+1))≥G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t)).L(\theta^{(t+1)}) = G(Q^{(t+2)}, \theta^{(t+1)}) \ge G(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t+1)}) \ge G(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t)}) = L(\theta^{(t)}).L(θ(t+1))=G(Q(t+2),θ(t+1))≥G(Q(t+1),θ(t+1))≥G(Q(t+1),θ(t))=L(θ(t)).
  • The first equality is the lemma’s “moreover” at iteration t+1t+1t+1: the E step’s beliefs make GGG equal to LLL.
  • The first inequality: Q(t+2)Q^{(t+2)}Q(t+2) maximizes G(⋅,θ(t+1))G(\cdot, \theta^{(t+1)})G(⋅,θ(t+1)) over Q\mathcal QQ, so it does at least as well as the particular matrix Q(t+1)Q^{(t+1)}Q(t+1).
  • The second inequality: θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)}θ(t+1) maximizes G(Q(t+1),⋅)G(Q^{(t+1)}, \cdot)G(Q(t+1),⋅), so it does at least as well as θ(t)\theta^{(t)}θ(t).
  • The last equality is the lemma’s “moreover” at iteration ttt.

In one sentence: each E step lifts GGG up to the log-likelihood, each M step lifts GGG further, so the log-likelihood can only climb. ■\blacksquare■

[diagram:em: built on the lesson page]

Since the log-likelihood never decreases, and (for a mixture where it is bounded above) a nondecreasing bounded sequence converges, the values L(θ(t))L(\theta^{(t)})L(θ(t)) settle down. What the theorem does not promise is that they settle at the global maximum: EM climbs, and a hill can be a local one.

Soft k-means

Let’s write EM out for a mixture of kkk Gaussians in which every covariance is the identity, Σy=I\Sigma_y = IΣy​=I, so the parameters are the shares ccc and the centres μ1,…,μk\mu_1, \dots, \mu_kμ1​,…,μk​.

E step. By Bayes’ rule, the probability of kind yyy given message xix_ixi​ is the joint probability divided by the total over kinds. The Gaussian normalizing constant (2π)d/2(2\pi)^{d/2}(2π)d/2 is the same for every kind and cancels:

Pθ(t)[Y=y∣X=xi]=1Zi cy(t)exp⁡(−12∥xi−μy(t)∥2).\mathbb P_{\theta^{(t)}}[Y = y \mid X = x_i] = \frac{1}{Z_i}\,c^{(t)}_y\exp\left(-\frac12\left\|x_i - \mu^{(t)}_y\right\|^2\right).Pθ(t)​[Y=y∣X=xi​]=Zi​1​cy(t)​exp(−21​​xi​−μy(t)​​2).
  • ∥xi−μy∥2\|x_i - \mu_y\|^2∥xi​−μy​∥2 is the ordinary squared distance from message iii to centre yyy (the stretched distance with Σ=I\Sigma = IΣ=I).
  • ZiZ_iZi​ is the normalization factor, ∑y′cy′exp⁡(−12∥xi−μy′∥2)\sum_{y'} c_{y'}\exp(-\frac12\|x_i - \mu_{y'}\|^2)∑y′​cy′​exp(−21​∥xi​−μy′​∥2), which makes the probabilities for message iii add up to 1.

In one sentence: each message belongs to each kind in proportion to the kind’s share times how close the message is to its centre. A message at length score 2.5, halfway between centres 1 and 4 with shares 0.7 and 0.3, belongs to the first kind with probability 0.7/(0.7+0.3)=0.70.7/(0.7 + 0.3) = 0.70.7/(0.7+0.3)=0.7, since the distances are equal.

M step. Write Qi,yQ_{i,y}Qi,y​ for the E step’s probabilities. Dropping constants that do not involve ccc or μ\muμ, the M step maximizes

∑i=1m∑y=1kQi,y(log⁡cy−12∥xi−μy∥2).\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{y=1}^{k} Q_{i,y}\left(\log c_y - \frac12\|x_i - \mu_y\|^2\right).i=1∑m​y=1∑k​Qi,y​(logcy​−21​∥xi​−μy​∥2).
  • Each term is log⁡Pθ[X=xi,Y=y]\log\mathbb P_\theta[X = x_i, Y = y]logPθ​[X=xi​,Y=y], which is log⁡cy−12∥xi−μy∥2−d2log⁡2π\log c_y - \frac12\|x_i - \mu_y\|^2 - \frac d2\log 2\pilogcy​−21​∥xi​−μy​∥2−2d​log2π, with the last constant dropped.

In one sentence: reward shares that are large where the beliefs are large, and centres that are close to the messages believed to belong to them. The centres and the shares appear in separate terms, so they can be optimized separately.

For a centre μy\mu_yμy​, set the gradient to zero. The gradient of −12∥xi−μy∥2-\frac12\|x_i - \mu_y\|^2−21​∥xi​−μy​∥2 with respect to μy\mu_yμy​ is xi−μyx_i - \mu_yxi​−μy​, so the condition is ∑iQi,y(xi−μy)=0\sum_i Q_{i,y}(x_i - \mu_y) = 0∑i​Qi,y​(xi​−μy​)=0; the objective is a concave quadratic in μy\mu_yμy​, so this point is the maximum. For the shares, the constraint that ccc is a probability vector needs more care, and you will prove the answer in the problems. The results are

μy=∑i=1mQi,y xi∑i=1mQi,y,cy=∑i=1mQi,y∑y′=1k∑i=1mQi,y′.\mu_y = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} Q_{i,y}\,x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} Q_{i,y}}, \qquad c_y = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} Q_{i,y}}{\sum_{y'=1}^{k}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Q_{i,y'}}.μy​=∑i=1m​Qi,y​∑i=1m​Qi,y​xi​​,cy​=∑y′=1k​∑i=1m​Qi,y′​∑i=1m​Qi,y​​.
  • μy\mu_yμy​ is a weighted average of all the messages, each weighted by how much it belongs to kind yyy.
  • ∑iQi,y\sum_i Q_{i,y}∑i​Qi,y​ is the total belief in kind yyy, a “soft count” of its messages; cyc_ycy​ is that soft count as a share of all mmm (the denominator equals mmm, since every row of QQQ adds up to 1).

In one sentence: move each centre to the weighted average of the messages, and set each share to the kind’s soft count over mmm. If three messages at 0, 1 and 2 belong to kind 1 with weights 1, 1 and 0.5, the new centre is (0+1+1)/2.5=0.8(0 + 1 + 1)/2.5 = 0.8(0+1+1)/2.5=0.8.

Compare this with the k-means algorithm of lesson 22. There, each message is assigned to its nearest centre, and each centre moves to the average of its assigned messages. Here, each message is assigned to every centre with a probability, and each centre moves to a weighted average over the entire sample. That is why EM for this model is called soft k-means.

[diagram:soft-kmeans: built on the lesson page]

SoftKMeans(x_1..x_m, k, T):
  choose initial c and μ_1..μ_k
  repeat T times (or until L stops improving):
    for i = 1..m:                      ▷ E step
      for y = 1..k:
        Q[i, y] ← c_y · exp(−½‖x_i − μ_y‖²)
      divide row i of Q by its sum
    for y = 1..k:                      ▷ M step
      n_y ← Σ_i Q[i, y]
      μ_y ← (Σ_i Q[i, y] x_i) / n_y
      c_y ← n_y / m
  return c, μ

Cost. Each E step computes mkmkmk squared distances in ddd dimensions, O(mkd)O(mkd)O(mkd) time; each M step is another weighted pass, O(mkd)O(mkd)O(mkd). So one iteration costs O(mkd)O(mkd)O(mkd) time, the same as one k-means iteration, and the memory is O(mk+kd)O(mk + kd)O(mk+kd) for QQQ and the centres (the data itself aside). In practice the exponentials are computed after subtracting each row’s largest exponent, so that exp⁡\expexp of a very negative number does not underflow to 0 for every kind at once.

Here is EM on the unlabelled archive, in one dimension: 140 personal notes around length score 1 and 60 newsletters around 4, with the kinds hidden. The snippet records the log-likelihood before each E step and checks that it never decreases.

import math, random
rng = random.Random(4)
xs = [rng.gauss(1, 1) for _ in range(140)]
xs += [rng.gauss(4, 1) for _ in range(60)]
c, mu, lls = [0.5, 0.5], [0.0, 0.5], []
def joint(x, y):
    g = math.exp(-(x - mu[y])**2 / 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
    return c[y] * g
for t in range(40):
    tot = [joint(x, 0) + joint(x, 1) for x in xs]
    lls.append(sum(math.log(v) for v in tot))
    Q = [[joint(x, y) / v for y in (0, 1)]
         for x, v in zip(xs, tot)]
    n = [sum(q[y] for q in Q) for y in (0, 1)]
    mu = [sum(q[y] * x for q, x in zip(Q, xs)) / n[y]
          for y in (0, 1)]
    c = [n[y] / len(xs) for y in (0, 1)]
print([round(v, 1) for v in lls[:4]], round(lls[-1], 1))
print(all(b >= a - 1e-9 for a, b in zip(lls, lls[1:])))
print([round(v, 2) for v in mu], [round(v, 2) for v in c])

It prints [-711.7, -414.6, -396.7, -387.4] -364.0, the log-likelihood climbing fast and then settling, then True, then [1.18, 3.98] [0.72, 0.28]: centres and shares close to the hidden truth (1 and 4, 0.7 and 0.3), found without a single label.

Build it yourself. In the standard library, for messages in Rd\mathbb R^dRd:

import math

X = [(0.0, 0.0), (0.5, 0.2), (0.1, 0.6), (4.0, 4.1),
     (3.6, 4.4), (4.3, 3.8), (0.3, 0.1), (4.1, 4.0)]

def soft_kmeans(X, mu, c, iters): ...
def log_likelihood(X, mu, c): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mu0, c0 = [(1.0, 0.0), (2.0, 3.0)], [0.5, 0.5]
    lls = []
    for t in range(1, 21):
        mu, c = soft_kmeans(X, mu0, c0, t)
        lls.append(log_likelihood(X, mu, c))
    assert all(b >= a - 1e-12 for a, b in zip(lls, lls[1:]))
    assert [round(v, 2) for v in sorted(c)] == [0.5, 0.5]
    assert round(lls[-1], 2) == -20.65
  1. Implement soft_kmeans (run iters EM iterations from the given start, identity covariances) and log_likelihood (the mixture log-likelihood with the (2π)d/2(2\pi)^{d/2}(2π)d/2 constant included).
  2. Start both centres at the same point. What happens, and which line of the monotonicity proof tells you EM can never escape?
  3. Replace the E step by a hard assignment to the most probable kind, and check that you have rebuilt k-means from lesson 22. Does the log-likelihood still never decrease?

What people get wrong

“A probability of 0 is just a very small probability.” In a product it is not small, it is a veto: one factor of 0 wipes out every other word’s evidence, and in a log it is minus infinity. For a rare word, maximum likelihood produces such a veto with probability at least one half, and its true risk is then infinite.

“Smoothing is a hack that makes the numbers look nicer.” Add-α\alphaα is regularized maximum likelihood, and add-one is exactly the predictive probability of a Bayesian with a uniform prior. It comes with a theorem: finite expected excess risk for every word, at the cost of a bias of at most α/(m+2α)\alpha/(m + 2\alpha)α/(m+2α).

“More pseudo-counts are always safer.” They make the log-loss certificate smaller but pull every estimate toward 1/21/21/2. In the fix, 20 pseudo-counts broke the accuracy certificate at 600 labels per kind.

“Naive Bayes assumes the words are independent.” It assumes they are independent given the label. “free” and “prize” are strongly correlated across all mail, simply because both are common in junk; the assumption is only that, within junk, one does not make the other more likely. That assumption is still usually false, and naive Bayes works anyway surprisingly often, because a classifier only needs the right side of the comparison, not the right probabilities.

“EM finds the maximum likelihood estimate.” The theorem only says it never goes downhill. It can stop at a local maximum, and a bad start (two identical centres, for instance) can keep it there forever.

“Maximum likelihood is a different principle from ERM.” It is ERM with the log loss, so it overfits when the class is too rich for the data, and a regularizer helps.

Recap and the next bug

  1. The generative approach assumes the data comes from a parametric model and estimates its parameters; the discriminative approach of the earlier lessons only learns to label.
  2. The maximum likelihood estimator picks the parameter that makes the training sequence most likely. For a yes/no feature it is the counted fraction k/mk/mk/m; for a Gaussian, the sample mean and the root of the average squared deviation.
  3. Maximum likelihood is ERM with the log loss −log⁡Pθ[x]-\log P_\theta[x]−logPθ​[x]. Its true risk is the entropy of the data plus the relative entropy from the truth to the model, which is zero only when the model is right.
  4. For a Gaussian centre the expected excess risk is 1/(2m)1/(2m)1/(2m). For a rare yes/no feature, maximum likelihood sets the estimate to 0 with probability at least one half when m≤log⁡2/(2θ⋆)m \le \log 2/(2\theta^\star)m≤log2/(2θ⋆), and its true risk is infinite: the bug.
  5. Pseudo-counts, θ^α=(k+α)/(m+2α)\hat\theta_\alpha = (k + \alpha)/(m + 2\alpha)θ^α​=(k+α)/(m+2α), are regularized maximum likelihood and, for α=1\alpha = 1α=1, the Bayesian prediction under a uniform prior. They keep the estimate within log⁡(2/δ)/(2m)+α/(m+2α)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)} + \alpha/(m + 2\alpha)log(2/δ)/(2m)​+α/(m+2α) of the truth and the expected excess risk below (m/4+α2)/(α(m+α))(m/4 + \alpha^2)/(\alpha(m + \alpha))(m/4+α2)/(α(m+α)).
  6. Naive Bayes assumes the features are independent given the label, cutting 2d2^d2d parameters to 2d+12d + 12d+1; trained by counting in O(md)O(md)O(md), it predicts in O(d)O(d)O(d). LDA assumes Gaussian classes with a shared covariance and produces a halfspace.
  7. EM handles latent variables by alternating soft assignments and refits; it is alternate maximization of GGG, so the log-likelihood never decreases. With identity covariances it is soft k-means.

Ines’s filter now ships with a certificate, and it is fast. But look at what it is made of. It keeps a parameter for every one of the 200 words in the dictionary, and the real dictionary has tens of thousands. Most of those words are noise: they appear about as often in junk as in keep, and every one of them adds a little random evidence to every decision, and two more numbers to estimate. And some of the most useful signals are not words at all: the ratio of links to text, a sender’s history, “prize” and “claim” appearing together. Which features should the filter keep, and could it build better ones than the ones it was given? That is the next lesson: feature selection and generation.

Concept check

Write your answers down before moving on to the next lesson, with your reasoning, not just the answer.

  1. The word “unsubscribe” appears in every one of the 300 junk messages your users labelled. What is its maximum likelihood estimate in junk, and what happens to Ines’s filter on a junk message that does not contain it? What does add-one smoothing estimate instead? Which part of the pseudo-count theorem covers this case, and why does it not matter which end of [0,1][0, 1][0,1] the true frequency is close to?
  2. In the proof that EM never decreases the likelihood, the chain has two equalities and two inequalities. Suppose your M step is only approximate: it returns some θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)}θ(t+1) with F(Q(t+1),θ(t+1))≥F(Q(t+1),θ(t))F(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t+1)}) \ge F(Q^{(t+1)}, \theta^{(t)})F(Q(t+1),θ(t+1))≥F(Q(t+1),θ(t)), but not the maximizer. Does the theorem still hold? Which link of the chain changes, and why is it still valid? What if instead the E step were approximate?
  3. A word appears in junk with true frequency θ⋆=0.001\theta^\star = 0.001θ⋆=0.001. (a) Up to what number of junk messages mmm does the rare-word theorem guarantee that maximum likelihood has infinite true risk with probability at least one half? (b) With m=1,000m = 1{,}000m=1,000 and add-one smoothing, what does the pseudo-count theorem bound the expected excess risk by? (c) With m=1,000m = 1{,}000m=1,000 and δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, how far from θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆ can the add-one estimate be, by part (a) of the theorem, and why is that bound so much worse than the bias alone?
